Research Proposal: Cross-Lingual Contrastive Retrieval for Low-Resource Neural
Machine Translation## Title
CREST-MT: Cross-Lingual Contrastive
Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning for Low-Resource Machine Translation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Neural machine translation (NMT) for low-resource language pairs suffers
from data sparsity. While massively multilingual pretrained models (e.g., mBART,
NLLB) provide a strong foundation, they are expensive to deploy and fine-tune,
and their coverage of truly low-resource languages remains uneven. Current
approaches either rely on large-scale back-translation (which introduces noise)
or on pivoting through a high-resource language (which compounds errors). There
is no established method that efficiently selects high-quality synthetic
training data from monolingual corpora without requiring a seed translation
system or a large teacher model.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Cross-lingual sentence embeddings, learned via a lightweight
contrastive objective on a small bilingual dictionary (≤5k entries), can
retrieve high-quality parallel sentence pairs from monolingual corpora to
augment a small seed parallel corpus. An NMT model fine-tuned on this augmented
data will outperform: (1) training on the seed corpus alone, (2) standard
back-translation augmentation, and (3) using generic multilingual sentence
encoders (e.g., LaBSE) for retrieval, particularly when the total compute budget
is ≤1 GPU-day.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1: Lightweight Cross-Lingual Retriever1. Input:5,000 word-level
translation pairs from a bilingual dictionary (or automatically induced via
unsupervised bilingual lexicon induction). Two large monolingual corpora (source
side: ~5M sentences, target side: ~5M sentences).

2 Encoder: A small dual-encoder Transformer (2 layers,256-dim hidden,4 heads —
≈6M parameters) initialized independently on source and target monolingual
data via masked language modeling (1 epoch each).
3 Contrastive alignment: For each dictionary entry, sample an equal number of
unrelated source/target words as negatives. Optimize with InfoNCE loss + a
margin of0.3. No back-translation or parallel data is needed.
4 Retrieval: Encode all sentences from both monolingual corpora with the
aligned encoder. For each source sentence, retrieve the top-5 target
sentences by cosine similarity. Apply a confidence threshold (≥0.7) to retain
only high-confidence pairs.

Stage2: NMT Fine-Tuning1. Seed parallel corpus:20k sentence pairs.

2 Augmented corpus: Seed + high-confidence retrieved pairs (expected
yield:50k–150k depending on language pair — accept50k as minimum).
3 Model:6-layer Transformer (512-dim,8-head encoder-decoder) — intentionally
kept small.
4 Training: Standard label-smoothed cross-entropy (label smoothing ε=0.1), Adam
(β₁=0.9, β₂=0.98), inverse sqrt learning rate scheduler (warmup4000 steps).
Batch size4096 tokens. Early stopping based on dev perplexity (patience5).1
GPU-day budget on a single A100.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Split | Size | Source |

|---|---|---| | Bilingual dictionary |5,000 pairs | Wiktionary / PanLex /
automatic induction | | Seed parallel (train) |20k pairs | JW300 or Tatoeba | |
Monolingual (source) |5M sentences | CommonCrawl / Leipzig Corpora | |
Monolingual (target) |5M sentences | CommonCrawl / Leipzig Corpora | | Dev |2k
pairs | FLORES-200 dev split | | Test |2k pairs | FLORES-200 devtest split |

Language pair: Gujarati → English (gu-en), a genuinely low-resource pair with
under100k publicly available parallel sentences. The same pipeline should also
be evaluated on a second pair (e.g., Kazakh → English) to ensure results are not
language-specific.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics- BLEU (sacrébleu signature:
nrefs:1|case:mixed|eff:no|tok:13a|smooth:exp) — primary metric- chrF++
(character-level) — secondary, captures morphologically faithful translations-
COMET (wmt22-comet-da) — neural metric for semantic adequacy- Retrieval
precision@1 on held-out bilingual dictionary entries (to validate the retriever
quality in Stage1)

• Effective augmentation yield: number of retrieved pairs above the confidence
thresholdAll NMT models are run with 3 random seeds. We report means with95%
bootstrap confidence intervals.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| # | Method | Key Difference from CREST-MT |

|---|---|---| | B1 | Seed-only fine-tuning | No data augmentation | | B2 | Seed
+ standard back-translation | Uses a target→source model to back-translate
target monolingual data | | B3 | Seed + LaBSE-based retrieval (Feng et al.,2022)
| Replaces our contrastive retriever with the publicly available LaBSE encoder |
| B4 | mBART-50 fine-tuned on seed (4 layers unfrozen) | Multilingual pretrained
baseline,4× parameter cost | | B5 | Random retrieval: seed + randomly paired
monolingual sentences | Upper bound on noise; controls for data quantity alone |
| B6 | Bilingual dictionary induction baseline: replaces the dictionary with an
automatically induced one (unsupervised) | Tests sensitivity to dictionary
quality |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. Retriever size: Remove contrastive alignment entirely (train on
word-level MLM only, no bilingual signal).

2 Confidence threshold: Vary the threshold (0.5,0.7,0.85,0.95) to measure
precision–recall trade-off on retrieved pairs.
3 Dictionary size: Reduce dictionary from5k →1k →200 entries to measure how
much bilingual signal the retriever needs.
4 Negative sampling strategy: Compare random negatives vs. in-batch negatives
vs. hard negative mining via TF-IDF similarity.
5 Monolingual data quantity: Subset source/target monolingual data from5M →500k
→50k sentences.
6 NMT model scale: Increase NMT to12-layer/1024-dim to test whether gains
persist in larger models.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation |

|---|---|---| | Retriever yields no high-confidence pairs (<50k) | Medium —
depends on how well dictionary covers the monolingual data | Fall back to a
weaker threshold (0.5) and filter by round-trip consistency instead; if still
<50k, report ablation (A2) to characterize the threshold boundary | | Augmented
data is too noisy and degrades BLEU | Low–Medium — random retrieval baseline
(B5) bounds noise, and contrastive retrieval should be better than random |
Measure per-pair confidence and stratify test-set BLEU by retrieval confidence
quartiles; if low-confidence pairs actively hurt, use confidence-weighted
training loss | | Dictionary quality is poor (many incorrect entries) | Low for
Wiktionary; Medium for automatically induced dictionaries | B6 ablation tests
this explicitly; if Wiktionary exists for the language pair, use it; if not,
report the induction baseline separately | | Gains appear only on small NMT
model, vanish at scale | Medium — larger models have stronger language priors
and may not benefit from extra data | Ablation A6 tests this directly; if gains
vanish, reframe contribution as "efficient retrieval for small models" | |
Computational budget (1 GPU-day) is insufficient | Low — the small encoder and
modest NMT are designed to fit this budget | Profile training step time; if
close to the limit, reduce monolingual data to2M sentences and cap NMT epochs
at30 | | Results are language-pair specific | Medium — gu-en may be easy due to
shared script in some domains, or hard due to limited data quality | Replicate
on a second language pair (kk-en) with distinct script and different data
sources; report both in the main paper |

**1. Title**
Iterative Semantic-Consistent Back-Translation (ISC-BT): Enhancing Low-Resource NMT via Cross-Lingual Embedding Alignment and Quality-Aware Filtering.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Neural Machine Translation (NMT) typically requires millions of parallel sentence pairs to achieve high fluency and accuracy. For the majority of the world’s languages (e.g., Yoruba, Quechua, or Wolof), such corpora do not exist. While standard Back-Translation (BT) utilizes monolingual data to bridge this gap, it often introduces significant noise and "hallucinations" into the training set when the initial translation model is weak. This leads to a feedback loop of poor quality. There is a critical need for a method that filters synthetic data based on semantic preservation rather than just surface-level fluency.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
Integrating a cross-lingual semantic consistency constraint—derived from a frozen, pre-trained multilingual encoder (e.g., LaBSE)—into the back-translation loop will significantly reduce the propagation of translation errors. Specifically, by filtering synthetic pairs that fall below a semantic similarity threshold and applying a consistency loss during fine-tuning, the model will achieve higher BLEU and COMET scores compared to vanilla back-translation.

**4. Method**
The workflow is divided into three distinct implementation phases:

*   **Phase 1: Warm-up.** Fine-tune a pre-trained multilingual model (e.g., mBART-50) on the available small-scale parallel data for the target language pair ($L_{src} \leftrightarrow L_{tgt}$).
*   **Phase 2: Semantic-Consistent Generation.**
    *   Use the backward model ($L_{tgt} \to L_{src}$) to translate a large corpus of monolingual $L_{tgt}$ data into synthetic $L_{src}'$.
    *   **Filtering:** Calculate the cosine similarity between the embeddings of the synthetic $L_{src}'$ and the original $L_{tgt}$ using the Language-Agnostic BERT Sentence Embedding (LaBSE). Discard pairs with a similarity score below a tuned threshold $\tau$.
*   **Phase 3: Iterative Fine-tuning.**
    *   Train the forward model ($L_{src} \to L_{tgt}$) on the combined gold and filtered synthetic data.
    *   **Regularization:** Introduce a "Semantic Consistency Loss" ($L_{sc}$) which minimizes the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the encoder hidden states of the synthetic source and the gold target, ensuring the model focuses on invariant semantic features.
*   **Phase 4: Iteration.** Repeat Phase 2 and 3 once more using the improved models to refine the synthetic corpus.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **Languages:** English-Yoruba (yo) and English-Quechua (qu).
*   **Data Source:** Use the **FLORES-200** dataset for evaluation (dev and test sets).
*   **Training Data:** Use the **JW300** corpus or **OPUS** for initial parallel data (limited to 50k pairs to simulate low-resource conditions) and the **NLLB Monolingual Cleaned** dataset for the back-translation source.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Primary:** BLEU (sacreBLEU implementation) and chrF++.
*   **Neural Metric:** COMET (Cross-lingual Optimized Metric for Evaluation of Translation), which correlates better with human judgment in low-resource settings.
*   **Semantic Drift:** Average LaBSE similarity between test source and model output.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Supervised mBART-50:** Fine-tuning on the limited parallel data only.
*   **Vanilla Back-Translation:** Standard iterative BT without semantic filtering or consistency loss.
*   **Pivot-based MT:** Using a high-resource related language (e.g., Spanish for Quechua) as an intermediary.

**8. Ablations**
*   **No Filtering:** Evaluate the impact of removing the LaBSE-based similarity filter.
*   **No Consistency Loss:** Evaluate the model using only the filtered data without the MSE regularization in the loss function.
*   **Fixed vs. Iterative:** Compare a single round of BT against the proposed two-iteration approach.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Domain Mismatch:** If the monolingual data is from a vastly different domain (e.g., news) than the parallel data (e.g., religious texts), the semantic filter may discard too much data. *Mitigation:* Use domain-adversarial training or ensure monolingual data diversity.
*   **Embedding Bias:** LaBSE itself might have lower performance on extremely rare languages. *Mitigation:* Validate LaBSE alignment on the small gold parallel set before proceeding.
*   **Computational Cost:** Iterative training and embedding generation are resource-intensive. *Mitigation:* Use 8-bit quantization for the LaBSE encoder and limit the synthetic corpus size to 5x the parallel corpus.

answer_a:
Research Proposal: Self-Specification Alignment for LLM-Generated Code##
Title
Self-Specification Alignment: Closing the Validation Loop for LLM Code
Generation Using Automatically Generated Behavioral Oracles

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based code generation is evaluated almost entirely on observed test
coverage — does the generated code pass the few unit tests that ship with the
benchmark (HumanEval, MBPP, etc.)? This creates a well-known gap: code can pass
the provided tests while being functionally incorrect on edge cases or failing
to align with the full natural-language specification. In real software
engineering, the gap between "passes tests" and "correct" is where bugs live.

Current approaches (pass@k, test-time repair) attempt to close this gap by
sampling many candidates or brute-force re-prompting on test failure, but they
never broaden the test oracle itself. The specification is only consulted by the
human providing the original tests — the LLM never generates a specification it
then holds itself accountable to.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis> H1: For a given programming problem described in natural language,
an LLM can generate a behavioral oracle (a set of property-based or
example-based tests) that is more complete than the small set of tests provided
in the benchmark, and that oracle can be used to detect and repair incorrect
solutions that pass the original tests.

▌ H2: This self-specification + self-repair loop improves functional
▌ correctness over the baseline pass@k on the original test set, with
▌ diminishing returns bounded by the quality of the LLM-generated oracle.

The key claim is that the marginal correctness signal of self-generated tests —
tests the model writes about its own spec — is positive relative to the original
test set, even though the model generates both the code and the tests.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal consists of three stages:

Stage1 — Conditional Test GenerationGiven a problem description (docstring +
signature + examples), prompt the LLM to generate k additional test cases that:

• Cover edge cases (empty input, boundary values, large inputs, type
mismatches)
• Exercise postconditions stated in the docstring- Include both positive
(should pass) and negative (should reject/invalid input) casesConstraints:
the generated tests must be executable and self-contained.

Stage2 — Self-Specification ValidationFor each candidate solution:

1 Run it against the original benchmark tests. If it fails → discard.
2 Run it against the self-generated tests from Stage1. If it fails → flag for
repair.
3 Metric: oracle disagreement rate — what fraction of candidates that pass
original tests are caught by self-generated tests?

Stage3 — Iterative Self-RepairFor every candidate that passes original tests but
fails self-generated tests:

• Return the failing test(s) + failure message to the LLM as a repair prompt.
• Generate a repaired candidate.
• Re-validate against both original and self-generated tests.
• Repeat up to N iterations (or until all tests pass).
• Measure: success rate of repair (fraction of flagged candidates that pass all
tests after repair), and added correctness (fraction of originally-passed
problems that are now correct on a held-out test set).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Language | Problems | Relevance |

|---|---|---|---| | HumanEval+ (Liu et al.,2023) | Python |164 | Extended tests
beyond original HumanEval; serves as ground-truth oracle | | MBPP+ (Liu et
al.,2023) | Python |399 | Another standard; extended tests | | CodeContests
(DeepMind,2022) | Python/C++ | ~10k | Harder problems with rich test suites |

Use HumanEval+/MBPP+ as primary (known ground-truth oracles). The original test
set (5–10 tests) serves as the "provided tests"; the extended tests (Liu et
al.'s hand-audited additions or self-generated) serve as the evaluation oracle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition |

|---|---| | pass@k | Fraction of problems solved by any of k samples using
original tests | | self-gap | Fraction of pass@k solutions that fail
self-generated tests (oracle disagreement) | | repair recovery | Fraction of
self-gap failures that are repaired to pass all tests | | added-correctness@k |
Fraction of problems that only become correct after self-specification + repair
(true positives) | | over-repair rate | Fraction of problems where self-repair
breaks a previously correct solution (regression) | | test oracle precision |
Fraction of self-generated test failures that correspond to actual errors (on
held-out ground truth) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. pass@k greedy — standard top-1 sampling, no repair.

2 pass@k sample — standard sampling (k=10,100,200).
3 self-repair (original tests only) — repair using only the original benchmark
tests (to isolate the value of additional self-generated tests).
4 LLM-as-judge (no execution) — ask the LLM whether the solution is correct,
without running tests; report as a soft ablation of the execution signal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations| Ablation | Question Answered |

|---|---| | No self-generated tests | Is the self-specification oracle adding
signal beyond just re-prompting? | | Self-generated tests from a different model
| Is the quality of self-generated tests model-dependent? (e.g., GPT-4o
generates tests, DeepSeek generates code) | | Single repair vs. multi-turn
repair | Does repair degrade after1–2 iterations (overfitting to generated
tests)? | | Docstring-only vs. docstring + signature + example | How much
specification context is needed to generate useful tests? | | Temperature
ablation on test generation | Does diverse test generation (high T) improve
oracle coverage? |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Circular validation — The LLM generates tests that
match its code bugs instead of the spec. If both code and tests share the same
blind spot, the oracle adds no signal → large self-gap is actually large
false-negative rate. Mitigation: measure precision on human-audited extended
tests (HumanEval+).

2 Over-repair / regressions — Repairing against self-generated tests breaks
correctness on the original tests or introduces new bugs. Mitigation: always
check original tests post-repair; report over-repair rate explicitly.
3 Specification underspecification — The docstring itself is ambiguous or
underspecified, so no amount of test generation can disambiguate it. The
method is bounded by the quality of the input specification. Mitigation:
filter problems where human annotators deem the spec unambiguous and report

**Title:** Graph-Augmented Iterative Refinement (GAIR): Enhancing Repository-Wide Code Refactoring via Static Analysis Feedback Loops

**Problem and Motivation**
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated proficiency in generating localized code snippets but frequently fail at repository-scale refactoring. When a developer modifies a function signature or moves a class in a large codebase, the change often necessitates cascading updates across multiple files. Current LLM-based agents often suffer from "contextual blindness," where they modify the target file correctly but fail to identify or update downstream dependencies, leading to compilation errors or broken API contracts. Existing RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) methods primarily rely on semantic similarity, which often misses structural dependencies critical for software integrity.

**Core Hypothesis**
Integrating a Static Analysis Call Graph (SACG) directly into the LLM’s reasoning loop—allowing the model to query structural dependencies before and after a code transformation—will significantly reduce "broken-dependency" regressions compared to standard text-based retrieval or long-context window models.

**Method**
The GAIR framework follows a three-stage iterative process:
1.  **Dependency Mapping:** For a given refactoring task (e.g., "Rename class X and update all usages"), the system uses a language server (LSP) to generate a local dependency graph of the affected symbols.
2.  **Context Construction:** The system populates the LLM's prompt with (a) the target code to be modified and (b) a structural summary of all files identified in the dependency map (e.g., function signatures and file paths).
3.  **Iterative Verification Loop:**
    *   The LLM proposes a set of multi-file edits.
    *   A static analysis tool (e.g., Tree-sitter or a compiler) checks for "undefined symbol" errors or signature mismatches.
    *   If errors are found, the error logs and the relevant nodes from the call graph are fed back to the LLM for a corrective pass.
    *   This continues until the code passes static verification or a maximum iteration limit is reached.

**Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **SWE-bench (Lite):** A subset of real-world GitHub issues that require multi-file edits.
*   **RefactorBench:** A synthetic dataset created by applying common refactoring patterns (extract method, move class, change signature) to popular open-source repositories (e.g., Django, Flask, Transformers) and verifying the ground truth via manual PRs.

**Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Success Rate (Pass@1):** Percentage of tasks where the final code passes all unit tests.
*   **Compilation Rate:** Percentage of generated solutions that are syntactically correct and resolve all internal dependencies.
*   **Dependency Recall:** The ratio of required file changes correctly identified by the model vs. the total files that needed modification for a successful refactor.
*   **Edit Distance (to Ground Truth):** Measuring how closely the structural changes match the human-authored PR.

**Baselines**
1.  **Vanilla GPT-4 / Claude 3.5 Sonnet:** Providing the full repository context (within token limits) without explicit structural guidance.
2.  **BM25 RAG:** A standard retrieval-augmented baseline that fetches files based on keyword similarity to the refactoring instruction.
3.  **RepoCoder:** A baseline that utilizes a similarity-based search-and-generate iteration without formal static analysis feedback.

**Ablations**
*   **No-Feedback Pass:** The model generates the refactor in one shot using the graph context but without the iterative verification loop.
*   **Text-only Feedback:** The model receives error logs from the compiler but no structural information from the call graph.
*   **Localized Graph:** Limiting the call graph to only immediate (1-hop) dependencies to test the necessity of deep dependency tracking.

**Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **State Space Explosion:** In highly coupled repositories, the dependency graph may be too large for the context window. *Mitigation:* Implement graph pruning to include only "high-probability" affected nodes.
*   **Dynamic Language Limitations:** For languages like Python, static analysis can be imprecise due to dynamic typing. *Mitigation:* Supplement static analysis with type hints and runtime execution traces where available.
*   **Computational Cost:** Multiple LLM calls per refactoring task increase latency and cost. *Mitigation:* Use a smaller "critic" model for the iterative verification and only call the "actor" model for major structural changes.

Research Proposal: Self-Specification Alignment for LLM-Generated Code##
Title
Self-Specification Alignment: Closing the Validation Loop for LLM Code
Generation Using Automatically Generated Behavioral Oracles

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based code generation is evaluated almost entirely on observed test
coverage — does the generated code pass the few unit tests that ship with the
benchmark (HumanEval, MBPP, etc.)? This creates a well-known gap: code can pass
the provided tests while being functionally incorrect on edge cases or failing
to align with the full natural-language specification. In real software
engineering, the gap between "passes tests" and "correct" is where bugs live.

Current approaches (pass@k, test-time repair) attempt to close this gap by
sampling many candidates or brute-force re-prompting on test failure, but they
never broaden the test oracle itself. The specification is only consulted by the
human providing the original tests — the LLM never generates a specification it
then holds itself accountable to.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis> H1: For a given programming problem described in natural language,
an LLM can generate a behavioral oracle (a set of property-based or
example-based tests) that is more complete than the small set of tests provided
in the benchmark, and that oracle can be used to detect and repair incorrect
solutions that pass the original tests.

▌ H2: This self-specification + self-repair loop improves functional
▌ correctness over the baseline pass@k on the original test set, with
▌ diminishing returns bounded by the quality of the LLM-generated oracle.

The key claim is that the marginal correctness signal of self-generated tests —
tests the model writes about its own spec — is positive relative to the original
test set, even though the model generates both the code and the tests.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal consists of three stages:

Stage1 — Conditional Test GenerationGiven a problem description (docstring +
signature + examples), prompt the LLM to generate k additional test cases that:

• Cover edge cases (empty input, boundary values, large inputs, type
mismatches)
• Exercise postconditions stated in the docstring- Include both positive
(should pass) and negative (should reject/invalid input) casesConstraints:
the generated tests must be executable and self-contained.

Stage2 — Self-Specification ValidationFor each candidate solution:

1 Run it against the original benchmark tests. If it fails → discard.
2 Run it against the self-generated tests from Stage1. If it fails → flag for
repair.
3 Metric: oracle disagreement rate — what fraction of candidates that pass
original tests are caught by self-generated tests?

Stage3 — Iterative Self-RepairFor every candidate that passes original tests but
fails self-generated tests:

• Return the failing test(s) + failure message to the LLM as a repair prompt.
• Generate a repaired candidate.
• Re-validate against both original and self-generated tests.
• Repeat up to N iterations (or until all tests pass).
• Measure: success rate of repair (fraction of flagged candidates that pass all
tests after repair), and added correctness (fraction of originally-passed
problems that are now correct on a held-out test set).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Language | Problems | Relevance |

|---|---|---|---| | HumanEval+ (Liu et al.,2023) | Python |164 | Extended tests
beyond original HumanEval; serves as ground-truth oracle | | MBPP+ (Liu et
al.,2023) | Python |399 | Another standard; extended tests | | CodeContests
(DeepMind,2022) | Python/C++ | ~10k | Harder problems with rich test suites |

Use HumanEval+/MBPP+ as primary (known ground-truth oracles). The original test
set (5–10 tests) serves as the "provided tests"; the extended tests (Liu et
al.'s hand-audited additions or self-generated) serve as the evaluation oracle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition |

|---|---| | pass@k | Fraction of problems solved by any of k samples using
original tests | | self-gap | Fraction of pass@k solutions that fail
self-generated tests (oracle disagreement) | | repair recovery | Fraction of
self-gap failures that are repaired to pass all tests | | added-correctness@k |
Fraction of problems that only become correct after self-specification + repair
(true positives) | | over-repair rate | Fraction of problems where self-repair
breaks a previously correct solution (regression) | | test oracle precision |
Fraction of self-generated test failures that correspond to actual errors (on
held-out ground truth) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. pass@k greedy — standard top-1 sampling, no repair.

2 pass@k sample — standard sampling (k=10,100,200).
3 self-repair (original tests only) — repair using only the original benchmark
tests (to isolate the value of additional self-generated tests).
4 LLM-as-judge (no execution) — ask the LLM whether the solution is correct,
without running tests; report as a soft ablation of the execution signal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations| Ablation | Question Answered |

|---|---| | No self-generated tests | Is the self-specification oracle adding
signal beyond just re-prompting? | | Self-generated tests from a different model
| Is the quality of self-generated tests model-dependent? (e.g., GPT-4o
generates tests, DeepSeek generates code) | | Single repair vs. multi-turn
repair | Does repair degrade after1–2 iterations (overfitting to generated
tests)? | | Docstring-only vs. docstring + signature + example | How much
specification context is needed to generate useful tests? | | Temperature
ablation on test generation | Does diverse test generation (high T) improve
oracle coverage? |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Circular validation — The LLM generates tests that
match its code bugs instead of the spec. If both code and tests share the same
blind spot, the oracle adds no signal → large self-gap is actually large
false-negative rate. Mitigation: measure precision on human-audited extended
tests (HumanEval+).

2 Over-repair / regressions — Repairing against self-generated tests breaks
correctness on the original tests or introduces new bugs. Mitigation: always
check original tests post-repair; report over-repair rate explicitly.
3 Specification underspecification — The docstring itself is ambiguous or
underspecified, so no amount of test generation can disambiguate it. The
method is bounded by the quality of the input specification. Mitigation:
filter problems where human annotators deem the spec unambiguous and report
results conditioned on specification clarity.
4 Test generation cost — Generating k test cases per problem × n samples ×
repair iterations is significantly more expensive than sampling alone.
Mitigation: report token cost per solved problem; treat this as a proposed
quality-cost tradeoff.
5 Model self-attribution bias — The model may be overly agreeable with its own
generated tests, failing to challenge its code against rigorous oracles. The
cross-model ablation (tests from model A, code from model B) tests this
directly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Proposed Experimental Protocol1. For each problem, generate self-specification
tests (k=20) from the docstring.

2 Draw100 code samples per problem (pass@k evaluation).
3 For each sample passing original tests: run self-generated tests; flag
failures.
4 Attempt repair (up to3 iterations) on each flagged candidate.
5 Evaluate final correctness against HumanEval+ extended tests (ground truth).
6 Report: pass@k (baseline), added-correctness (method), self-gap, repair
recovery, over-repair rate, token cost per problem.

Research Proposal: Addressing Accuracy Issues in Automated LLM Evaluation---

Title
Calibrated Ensemble Evaluation (CEE): Improving LLM-as-a-Judge Accuracy
through Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Model Deliberation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based automated evaluators ("LLM-as-a-judge") are the dominant method
for evaluating open-ended text generation at scale, but suffer from four
well-documented accuracy issues:

1 Systematic biases — position bias (preferring first or second response),
verbosity bias (preferring longer outputs), and self-enhancement bias
(preferring outputs from models similar to the judge).
2 No uncertainty quantification — standard practice returns a point estimate
(score or preference) with no confidence, making it impossible to know when
the judge is uncertain vs confident.
3 Low inter-rater reliability — agreement between LLM judges and human raters
varies wildly across domains (Spearman ρ ranges from0.3 on creative writing
to0.7 on factual QA).
4 Rubric brittleness — even with detailed rubrics, LLM judges often fail to
follow multi-criteria instructions consistently, collapsing dimensions or
ignoring criteria.

The core unmet need is an evaluation framework that produces trustworthy scores
— scores that are calibrated, debiased, and accompanied by uncertainty — rather
than simply fast scores.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Decomposing evaluation into atomic quality criteria, aggregating
judgments from multiple diverse evaluator LLMs with explicit uncertainty
estimation, and calibrating the resulting scores against a small human-annotated
set will significantly improve accuracy — defined as Spearman rank correlation
with held-out human judgments — over the standard single-model, single-pass,
holistic-judgment baseline, while also reducing known biases (position,
verbosity) and providing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method (3-stage pipeline)

Stage1: Atomic Criterion DecompositionInstead of asking a judge for a single
"overall quality" score (which collapses heterogeneous dimensions), decompose
evaluation into6 atomic rubrics:

#  Criterion              Definition
1  Relevance              Does the response address the prompt directly?
2  Correctness            Are factual claims accurate? (for knowledge tasks)
3  Coherence              Is the response logically structured and internally
consistent?
4  Completeness           Does the response cover the scope requested?
5  Conciseness            Is the response free of unnecessary verbosity?
6  Instruction Following  Does the response obey format, length, and style
constraints?

Each criterion is scored on a1–5 Likert scale by each evaluator model, using a
criterion-specific prompt that includes the rubric definition, the prompt, and
the response. This prevents any single criterion from dominating.

Stage2: Multi-Model Panel with UncertaintyQuery a panel of K =3 to5 diverse LLM
evaluators (from different model families, e.g., GPT-4o, Claude3.5 Sonnet,
Llama370B, Gemini2.0 Flash, Mistral Large). Each model scores each response on
all6 criteria.

For each (model, criterion, response) triple, also extract the log-probability
of the score token(s) as a proxy for the model's confidence in that judgment.
This gives a per-criterion confidence weight.

Stage3: Calibration LayerUsing a held-out calibration set of N =500–1,000
examples with human ratings on the same6 criteria (collected from3 annotators
per example):

1 Score Aggregation: Per criterion, compute a confidence-weighted average
across models: s_c = Σ_i w_i_c * score_i_c / Σ_i w_i_c where w_i_c =
exp(logprob_i_c) is model i's confidence on criterion c.
2 Bias Correction: Fit a small logistic regression or isotonic regression per
criterion to map the aggregated score s_c to a calibrated score ŝ_c that
minimizes expected calibration error against human ratings.
3 Uncertainty Output: For each response, output both the calibrated score
vector ŝ ∈ [1,5]^6 and a per-criterion uncertainty interval derived from the
weighted variance across the panel.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Dataset | Use | Size | Human Annotations |

|---------|-----|------|-------------------| | MT-Bench | Primary evaluation |80
multi-turn questions,3,360 model outputs | Human preference + pairwise ratings
(published) | | Chatbot Arena (subset) | Primary evaluation |10K randomly
sampled comparisons | Human preference votes (public) | | FLASK | Fine-grained
evaluation | ~1,700 model outputs | Human ratings on12 fine-grained dimensions |
| ShareGPT + rubric annotation | Calibration set |500 examples,3 annotators/ex |
Collected fresh (6 atomic criteria + overall) | | AlpacaEval2.0 | OOD test |805
examples | Length-controlled win rates (indirect human signal) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | What it measures | Target |

|--------|-----------------|--------| | Spearman ρ (with human scores) | Rank
correlation — primary metric | >0.65 (vs ~0.50–0.55 for GPT-4 baseline on
creative/ open-ended tasks) | | Exact + Adjacent Agreement | Score-level match
with humans | >60% exact +85% adjacent | | Position Bias Rate | % of trials
where swapping A/B order flips the preference | <5% (vs ~15–20% for single-model
judges) | | Verbosity Correlation | Pearson r between predicted score and
response length (log tokens) | |r| <0.10 (vs ~0.35 for rubric-free judges) | |
Expected Calibration Error (ECE) | Binned calibration of confidence vs accuracy
| <0.08 | | Test-Retest Consistency | Variance across3 independent runs on same
input | σ² <0.02 per criterion | | Cost per Evaluation | API cost per evaluation
@ inference time | Report in USD for transparency |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Why chosen |

|----------|-------------|------------| | GPT-4-as-a-judge (holistic) | Single
GPT-4 call scoring "overall quality"1–5 | De facto standard in most LLM
evaluation pipelines | | GPT-4-as-a-judge (with rubric) | Same model, but with
the6 atomic criteria in prompt | Controls for rubric decomposition effect alone
| | PairRM | Trained pairwise reward model (based on Llama) | Representative of
trained, task-specific evaluators | | JudgeLM | Fine-tuned evaluator on100K
human judgments | Strongest published fine-tuned baseline | | Majority Vote (3x)
| Same model (GPT-4) called3 times, majority vote | Controls for the effect of
repeated sampling alone | | Humans (held out) | Human judgment on held-out test
set | Upper-bound oracle (no automated evaluation is expected to match this, but
it anchors the comparison) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations
Each ablation removes or varies one component of CEE while holding
everything else fixed, tested on the MT-Bench test set:

Ablation                 Variation                  What it isolates
Panel size               K =1 vs3 vs5 models        Value of model diversity
Criterion decomposition  Replace6 criteria with     Value of atomic rubric
single holistic "overall"  structure
judgment
Uncertainty weighting    Replace                    Value of log-prob
confidence-weighted        confidence signal
average with uniform
average
Calibration layer        Remove calibration (use    Value of human-anchored
raw aggregated scores)     calibration
Model diversity          Same-family panel (GPT-4o  Value of cross-family
×3) vs cross-family        diversity vs repeated
(GPT-4o + Claude + Llama)  sampling

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation |

|-------------|-----------|------------| | Calibration overfitting — the
calibration layer overfits to the small (500-example) human set and degrades on
OOD distributions like AlpacaEval | Medium | Use regularization (isotonic
regression with smoothing); report OOD performance separately; scale calibration
set to1,000 if budget permits | | Model collinearity — diverse models produce
correlated errors on the same failure cases (e.g., all miss subtle factual
errors in stylized text) | Medium-High | Analyze error correlation matrix across
models; if collinearity is high (>0.8 across all pairs), consider subsampling to
the two most independent models | | Criterion decomposition misses holistic
qualities — atomic rubrics fail to capture emergent dimensions (interestingness,
novelty, tone) that drive human preferences | Medium | Add a7th "overall
gestalt" criterion alongside atomic ones; check whether the holistic dimension
is needed for high human correlation via ablation | | Computational cost — K ×6
API calls per evaluation (e.g.,5 ×6 =30 calls) is15–30× more expensive than a
single-judge baseline, limiting practical adoption | High | Accept cost as a
trade-off for research-phase accuracy; report cost per evaluation; investigate
whether pruning to the top-2 criteria after a pilot study can reduce calls3×
with minimal accuracy loss | | Rubric leakage — models exhibit new
criterion-specific biases (e.g., always giving "conciseness" low scores to long
but good answers) | Medium | Exploratory analysis of per-criterion score
distributions; adjust rubric wording in a small pilot (N=50) before finalizing |
| Human annotation bottleneck — collecting500 ×6 ×3 ≈9,000 reliable
atomic-criterion annotations is expensive and slow | High | Use existing FLASK
dataset (already has fine-grained annotations) to bootstrap; only collect ~200
fresh annotations for the calibration held-out set | | Log-prob confidence is
poorly calibrated — score-token log-probs may not reflect true judgment
confidence, especially under sampling temperature >0 | Medium | Set temperature
to0 for evaluation calls; if log-probs still unreliable, replace with
self-reported confidence ("How confident are you in this score on a1-5 scale?")
as an alternative confidence signal |

### 1. Title
**Multi-Perspective Reasoning Calibration (MPRC): Improving LLM-as-a-Judge Accuracy via Structured Rationalization and Uncertainty-Aware Weighting**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Automated evaluation using Large Language Models (LLM-as-a-judge) is the current standard for scaling LLM benchmarking. However, this approach suffers from significant reliability issues, including:
*   **Positional Bias:** Favoring the first response in pairwise comparisons.
*   **Verbosity Bias:** Assigning higher scores to longer responses regardless of quality.
*   **Self-Preference Bias:** Favoring outputs that mirror the evaluator’s own stylistic patterns.
*   **Lack of Interpretability:** Direct scoring often provides a "black box" number without a verifiable logical trail.

Addressing these issues is critical for the development of alignment techniques (like RLHF) that rely on automated feedback loops.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
By forcing an evaluator LLM to decompose its judgment into structured, independent dimensions (e.g., logical correctness, adherence to constraints, and stylistic tone) and weighting these scores by their cross-trial consistency (uncertainty), we can significantly increase the correlation between automated scores and expert human judgments compared to monolithic scoring.

### 4. Method
The MPRC framework operates in four distinct phases:
1.  **Structured Rubric Decomposition:** Instead of a single prompt, the evaluator is provided with a multi-dimensional rubric. For each dimension, the model must generate a "Reasoning Trace" before assigning a numerical sub-score.
2.  **Cross-Perspective Perturbation:** The evaluation is run across three distinct personas (e.g., "Technical Auditor," "Creative Critic," and "General User") to mitigate individual model biases.
3.  **Uncertainty Estimation:** Each evaluation is sampled $N$ times at temperature $T > 0$. The variance in sub-scores serves as a proxy for evaluation uncertainty.
4.  **Calibrated Aggregation:** The final score is calculated using a weighted average where dimensions with high variance (low confidence) are down-weighted, and dimensions with high consistency are prioritized. If total uncertainty exceeds a threshold, the sample is flagged for human intervention.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **LMSYS Chatbot Arena Conversations:** Use the publicly available human preference dataset.
*   **MT-Bench:** A set of 80 high-quality multi-turn questions across categories (coding, reasoning, etc.) with human-expert gold labels.
*   **CritiqueBench:** To specifically test the model's ability to identify flaws in reasoning.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Human Agreement (Primary):** Spearman and Pearson correlation coefficients between MPRC scores and human ground-truth scores.
*   **Pairwise Accuracy:** The percentage of times the system correctly identifies the human-preferred winner in a side-by-side comparison.
*   **Bias Sensitivity:** Measuring the change in score when swapping the order of responses (Positional Bias) or artificially inflating length (Verbosity Bias).

### 7. Baselines
*   **Direct Prompting (GPT-4/Claude 3.5):** Standard "Rate this on a scale of 1-10" approach.
*   **G-Eval:** A state-of-the-art framework using CoT and weighted probabilities.
*   **Prometheus:** An open-source model specifically fine-tuned for evaluation tasks.

### 8. Ablations
*   **No Reasoning Trace:** Evaluating the impact of removing the CoT requirement.
*   **No Multi-Perspective:** Using only a single "General" persona.
*   **Uniform Weighting:** Comparing the uncertainty-aware weighting against a simple arithmetic mean of sub-scores.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Reasoning-Score Mismatch:** The model may generate a logical reasoning trace that points to a "Fail" but still output a high numerical score (hallucinated justification).
*   **Computational Overhead:** Running multiple personas and $N$ iterations significantly increases API costs and latency.
*   **Systemic Bias:** If all personas share the same underlying base model (e.g., all are variants of GPT-4), they may share the same blind spots, rendering the "multi-perspective" approach less effective. To mitigate this, the method should ideally use a mix of model families (e.g., Llama-3 and Claude).

*   **Lack of Interpretability:** Direct scoring often provides a "black box" number without a verifiable logical trail.

Addressing these issues is critical for the development of alignment techniques (like RLHF) that rely on automated feedback loops.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
By forcing an evaluator LLM to decompose its judgment into structured, independent dimensions (e.g., logical correctness, adherence to constraints, and stylistic tone) and weighting these scores by their cross-trial consistency (uncertainty), we can significantly increase the correlation between automated scores and expert human judgments compared to monolithic scoring.

### 4. Method
The MPRC framework operates in four distinct phases:
1.  **Structured Rubric Decomposition:** Instead of a single prompt, the evaluator is provided with a multi-dimensional rubric. For each dimension, the model must generate a "Reasoning Trace" before assigning a numerical sub-score.
2.  **Cross-Perspective Perturbation:** The evaluation is run across three distinct personas (e.g., "Technical Auditor," "Creative Critic," and "General User") to mitigate individual model biases.
3.  **Uncertainty Estimation:** Each evaluation is sampled $N$ times at temperature $T > 0$. The variance in sub-scores serves as a proxy for evaluation uncertainty.
4.  **Calibrated Aggregation:** The final score is calculated using a weighted average where dimensions with high variance (low confidence) are down-weighted, and dimensions with high consistency are prioritized. If total uncertainty exceeds a threshold, the sample is flagged for human intervention.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **LMSYS Chatbot Arena Conversations:** Use the publicly available human preference dataset.
*   **MT-Bench:** A set of 80 high-quality multi-turn questions across categories (coding, reasoning, etc.) with human-expert gold labels.
*   **CritiqueBench:** To specifically test the model's ability to identify flaws in reasoning.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Human Agreement (Primary):** Spearman and Pearson correlation coefficients between MPRC scores and human ground-truth scores.
*   **Pairwise Accuracy:** The percentage of times the system correctly identifies the human-preferred winner in a side-by-side comparison.
*   **Bias Sensitivity:** Measuring the change in score when swapping the order of responses (Positional Bias) or artificially inflating length (Verbosity Bias).

### 7. Baselines
*   **Direct Prompting (GPT-4/Claude 3.5):** Standard "Rate this on a scale of 1-10" approach.
*   **G-Eval:** A state-of-the-art framework using CoT and weighted probabilities.
*   **Prometheus:** An open-source model specifically fine-tuned for evaluation tasks.

### 8. Ablations
*   **No Reasoning Trace:** Evaluating the impact of removing the CoT requirement.
*   **No Multi-Perspective:** Using only a single "General" persona.
*   **Uniform Weighting:** Comparing the uncertainty-aware weighting against a simple arithmetic mean of sub-scores.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Reasoning-Score Mismatch:** The model may generate a logical reasoning trace that points to a "Fail" but still output a high numerical score (hallucinated justification).
*   **Computational Overhead:** Running multiple personas and $N$ iterations significantly increases API costs and latency.
*   **Systemic Bias:** If all personas share the same underlying base model (e.g., all are variants of GPT-4), they may share the same blind spots, rendering the "multi-perspective" approach less effective. To mitigate this, the method should ideally use a mix of model families (e.g., Llama-3 and Claude).

Research Proposal: Addressing Accuracy Issues in Automated LLM Evaluation---

Title
Calibrated Ensemble Evaluation (CEE): Improving LLM-as-a-Judge Accuracy
through Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Model Deliberation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based automated evaluators ("LLM-as-a-judge") are the dominant method
for evaluating open-ended text generation at scale, but suffer from four
well-documented accuracy issues:

1 Systematic biases — position bias (preferring first or second response),
verbosity bias (preferring longer outputs), and self-enhancement bias
(preferring outputs from models similar to the judge).
2 No uncertainty quantification — standard practice returns a point estimate
(score or preference) with no confidence, making it impossible to know when
the judge is uncertain vs confident.
3 Low inter-rater reliability — agreement between LLM judges and human raters
varies wildly across domains (Spearman ρ ranges from0.3 on creative writing
to0.7 on factual QA).
4 Rubric brittleness — even with detailed rubrics, LLM judges often fail to
follow multi-criteria instructions consistently, collapsing dimensions or
ignoring criteria.

The core unmet need is an evaluation framework that produces trustworthy scores
— scores that are calibrated, debiased, and accompanied by uncertainty — rather
than simply fast scores.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Decomposing evaluation into atomic quality criteria, aggregating
judgments from multiple diverse evaluator LLMs with explicit uncertainty
estimation, and calibrating the resulting scores against a small human-annotated
set will significantly improve accuracy — defined as Spearman rank correlation
with held-out human judgments — over the standard single-model, single-pass,
holistic-judgment baseline, while also reducing known biases (position,
verbosity) and providing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method (3-stage pipeline)

Stage1: Atomic Criterion DecompositionInstead of asking a judge for a single
"overall quality" score (which collapses heterogeneous dimensions), decompose
evaluation into6 atomic rubrics:

#  Criterion              Definition
1  Relevance              Does the response address the prompt directly?
2  Correctness            Are factual claims accurate? (for knowledge tasks)
3  Coherence              Is the response logically structured and internally
consistent?
4  Completeness           Does the response cover the scope requested?
5  Conciseness            Is the response free of unnecessary verbosity?
6  Instruction Following  Does the response obey format, length, and style
constraints?

Each criterion is scored on a1–5 Likert scale by each evaluator model, using a
criterion-specific prompt that includes the rubric definition, the prompt, and
the response. This prevents any single criterion from dominating.

Stage2: Multi-Model Panel with UncertaintyQuery a panel of K =3 to5 diverse LLM
evaluators (from different model families, e.g., GPT-4o, Claude3.5 Sonnet,
Llama370B, Gemini2.0 Flash, Mistral Large). Each model scores each response on
all6 criteria.

For each (model, criterion, response) triple, also extract the log-probability
of the score token(s) as a proxy for the model's confidence in that judgment.
This gives a per-criterion confidence weight.

Stage3: Calibration LayerUsing a held-out calibration set of N =500–1,000
examples with human ratings on the same6 criteria (collected from3 annotators
per example):

1 Score Aggregation: Per criterion, compute a confidence-weighted average
across models: s_c = Σ_i w_i_c * score_i_c / Σ_i w_i_c where w_i_c =
exp(logprob_i_c) is model i's confidence on criterion c.
2 Bias Correction: Fit a small logistic regression or isotonic regression per
criterion to map the aggregated score s_c to a calibrated score ŝ_c that
minimizes expected calibration error against human ratings.
3 Uncertainty Output: For each response, output both the calibrated score
vector ŝ ∈ [1,5]^6 and a per-criterion uncertainty interval derived from the
weighted variance across the panel.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Dataset | Use | Size | Human Annotations |

|---------|-----|------|-------------------| | MT-Bench | Primary evaluation |80
multi-turn questions,3,360 model outputs | Human preference + pairwise ratings
(published) | | Chatbot Arena (subset) | Primary evaluation |10K randomly
sampled comparisons | Human preference votes (public) | | FLASK | Fine-grained
evaluation | ~1,700 model outputs | Human ratings on12 fine-grained dimensions |
| ShareGPT + rubric annotation | Calibration set |500 examples,3 annotators/ex |
Collected fresh (6 atomic criteria + overall) | | AlpacaEval2.0 | OOD test |805
examples | Length-controlled win rates (indirect human signal) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | What it measures | Target |

|--------|-----------------|--------| | Spearman ρ (with human scores) | Rank
correlation — primary metric | >0.65 (vs ~0.50–0.55 for GPT-4 baseline on
creative/ open-ended tasks) | | Exact + Adjacent Agreement | Score-level match
with humans | >60% exact +85% adjacent | | Position Bias Rate | % of trials
where swapping A/B order flips the preference | <5% (vs ~15–20% for single-model
judges) | | Verbosity Correlation | Pearson r between predicted score and
response length (log tokens) | |r| <0.10 (vs ~0.35 for rubric-free judges) | |
Expected Calibration Error (ECE) | Binned calibration of confidence vs accuracy
| <0.08 | | Test-Retest Consistency | Variance across3 independent runs on same
input | σ² <0.02 per criterion | | Cost per Evaluation | API cost per evaluation
@ inference time | Report in USD for transparency |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Why chosen |

|----------|-------------|------------| | GPT-4-as-a-judge (holistic) | Single
GPT-4 call scoring "overall quality"1–5 | De facto standard in most LLM
evaluation pipelines | | GPT-4-as-a-judge (with rubric) | Same model, but with
the6 atomic criteria in prompt | Controls for rubric decomposition effect alone
| | PairRM | Trained pairwise reward model (based on Llama) | Representative of
trained, task-specific evaluators | | JudgeLM | Fine-tuned evaluator on100K
human judgments | Strongest published fine-tuned baseline | | Majority Vote (3x)
| Same model (GPT-4) called3 times, majority vote | Controls for the effect of
repeated sampling alone | | Humans (held out) | Human judgment on held-out test
set | Upper-bound oracle (no automated evaluation is expected to match this, but
it anchors the comparison) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations
Each ablation removes or varies one component of CEE while holding
everything else fixed, tested on the MT-Bench test set:

Ablation                 Variation                  What it isolates
Panel size               K =1 vs3 vs5 models        Value of model diversity
Criterion decomposition  Replace6 criteria with     Value of atomic rubric
single holistic "overall"  structure
judgment
Uncertainty weighting    Replace                    Value of log-prob
confidence-weighted        confidence signal
average with uniform
average
Calibration layer        Remove calibration (use    Value of human-anchored
raw aggregated scores)     calibration
Model diversity          Same-family panel (GPT-4o  Value of cross-family
×3) vs cross-family        diversity vs repeated
(GPT-4o + Claude + Llama)  sampling

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation |

|-------------|-----------|------------| | Calibration overfitting — the
calibration layer overfits to the small (500-example) human set and degrades on
OOD distributions like AlpacaEval | Medium | Use regularization (isotonic
regression with smoothing); report OOD performance separately; scale calibration
set to1,000 if budget permits | | Model collinearity — diverse models produce
correlated errors on the same failure cases (e.g., all miss subtle factual
errors in stylized text) | Medium-High | Analyze error correlation matrix across
models; if collinearity is high (>0.8 across all pairs), consider subsampling to
the two most independent models | | Criterion decomposition misses holistic
qualities — atomic rubrics fail to capture emergent dimensions (interestingness,
novelty, tone) that drive human preferences | Medium | Add a7th "overall
gestalt" criterion alongside atomic ones; check whether the holistic dimension
is needed for high human correlation via ablation | | Computational cost — K ×6
API calls per evaluation (e.g.,5 ×6 =30 calls) is15–30× more expensive than a
single-judge baseline, limiting practical adoption | High | Accept cost as a
trade-off for research-phase accuracy; report cost per evaluation; investigate
whether pruning to the top-2 criteria after a pilot study can reduce calls3×
with minimal accuracy loss | | Rubric leakage — models exhibit new
criterion-specific biases (e.g., always giving "conciseness" low scores to long
but good answers) | Medium | Exploratory analysis of per-criterion score
distributions; adjust rubric wording in a small pilot (N=50) before finalizing |
| Human annotation bottleneck — collecting500 ×6 ×3 ≈9,000 reliable
atomic-criterion annotations is expensive and slow | High | Use existing FLASK
dataset (already has fine-grained annotations) to bootstrap; only collect ~200
fresh annotations for the calibration held-out set | | Log-prob confidence is

confidence, especially under sampling temperature >0 | Medium | Set temperature
to0 for evaluation calls; if log-probs still unreliable, replace with
self-reported confidence ("How confident are you in this score on a1-5 scale?")
as an alternative confidence signal |

Research Proposal: Multi-Agent LLM Systems for Clinical Trial Eligibility
Screening## Title
TrialMatch: A Structured Multi-Agent Debate Framework for
Zero-Shot Clinical Trial Eligibility Screening

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Clinical trial enrollment is the bottleneck of medical research.
Eligibility screening — determining whether a patient's unstructured EHR notes
satisfy a trial's inclusion/exclusion criteria — is currently performed manually
by coordinators. This is slow, error-prone, and does not scale to the ~400,000
trials on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Single-pass LLM prompting achieves ~70–75% F1 on eligibility classification
(TrialGPT,2024), but suffers from two issues: (a) it hallucinates criterion
matches for ambiguous or missing data, and (b) it does not handle contradictory
criteria across multiple trials for the same patient.

Open question: Can a multi-agent debate architecture, where specialized agents
argue for and against each criterion, outperform a single monolithic LLM on this
task?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A multi-agent debate system — where one agent argues for criterion
satisfaction (citing specific evidence), a second argues against, and a judge
agent synthesizes the final decision — will improve F1 by ≥5 points over a
single-pass LLM with equal total inference cost, because forced adversarial
reasoning reduces hallucination on borderline criteria.

Null hypothesis: Multi-agent debate does not significantly outperform
single-pass prompting when both use the same backbone LLM and comparable token
budgets.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Architecture: TrialMatchThe system operates in three stages per
patient-trial pair:

1 Evidence Extraction: An extractor agent reads the patient note + trial
criteria and produces a structured table mapping each criterion to the spans
of text that are relevant (or marks the criterion as "no evidence in note").
2 Adversarial Debate (per criterion):

• Pro Agent — given the criterion and extracted evidence, argues why the
patient meets this criterion.
• Con Agent — given the same evidence, argues why the patient does not meet it.
• Each agent is temperature-decayed (T=0.7 →0.3) over3 rounds; they see each
other's arguments.

3 Aggregation & Prediction:

• Judge Agent — reads the debate transcripts for all criteria and produces:
• A binary eligibility decision (eligible / ineligible)
• A confidence score - Citations to specific spans in the original
noteBackbone: Llama-3.1-70B (or a similarly capable open model), quantized to
allow multi-agent rollouts on a single A100.

Prompt structure: Each agent is prompted with a role persona (e.g., "You are a
conservative clinical reviewer who requires explicit documentation before
approving") to ensure separation of perspectives.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Primary: TrialGPT benchmark (Jin et al.,2024) —183 patient
summaries (from TREC Clinical Trials) and3,500+ trial-criterion pairs with
expert-annotated eligibility labels. This is the standard zero-shot benchmark.

Secondary (robustness): N2C22018 (Adverse Drug Events cohort) — convert the ADE
extraction task into criterion-style screening for a drug trial; measure
cross-dataset transfer.

Validation method:5-fold patient-level cross-validation on TrialGPT. No patient
appears in both train and test folds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Rationale |

|---|---| | Macro F1 (primary) | Balanced measure for binary eligibility;
primary metric in TrialGPT | | Criterion-level accuracy | Per-criterion match vs
annotator labels (from TrialGPT's fine-grained labels) | | Precision vs Recall
tradeoff | Important for clinical use — false positives (enrolling an ineligible
patient) are costlier than false negatives | | Mean confidence calibration (ECE)
| Judge confidence should correlate with correctness | | Debate round
convergence | Does additional debate rounds (>3) change the final decision?
(sensitivity analysis) | | Token cost | Total tokens consumed per patient-trial
pair (runtime cost matters for deployment) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Single-pass LLM (same backbone, same evidence extraction step, no
debate) — direct ablation2. TrialGPT (Jin et al.,2024) — strongest published
zero-shot baseline3. Chain-of-Thought prompting on the same backbone — controls
for reasoning depth4. Self-consistency (Wang et al.,2023) with5 samples —
controls for ensemble effect vs. structured debate5. Random majority (predict
the majority class per trial) — sanity floorAll baselines share the same
evidence extraction stage and backbone model for fair comparison.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. No debate → single-pass LLM (this is baseline1 above)

2 Single-agent self-consistency (same number of forward passes as debate, but
no adversarial structure) — isolates the benefit of adversarial reasoning vs.
mere sampling3. Judge only, no pro/con (judge sees evidence directly) —
isolates the value of debate4. Debate without role personas (both agents
prompted as neutral reviewers) — tests whether forced role separation
matters5. Temperature ablation (fixed high vs. fixed low vs. decay schedule)
3 Backbone size (8B vs.70B) — does debate help smaller models more?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation |

|---|---| | Both pro and con hallucinate — debate converges on wrong facts
because both agents invent evidence | Evidence extraction stage is constrained
to quote spans only; agents cannot fabricate new facts | | Judge favors
pro/consistently — positional bias or role bias in the judge | Swap agent order
randomly; test two judge prompts (neutral; "prefer inclusion"; "prefer
exclusion") | | Token cost is prohibitive — multi-agent debate uses3–5× more
tokens than single-pass | Measure cost explicitly; report F1 per token. If gain
is <5 points, single-pass is economically preferable | | No improvement on easy
criteria — debate only helps borderline cases, which are rare (~15% of criteria)
| Report separately on "easy" (both agents initially agree) vs "hard" criteria;
overall F1 gain may be diluted | | Agent personas polarize unrecoverably — pro
and con become entrenched and never converge | Hard-limit at3 rounds; judge
always has the final say regardless of agreement | | Dataset leakage — LLM was
pre-trained on ClinicalTrials.gov or MIMIC notes | Use a held-out set of recent
trials (past12 months, beyond training cutoff); check for exact matches | |
Cross-dataset transfer fails — N2C2 performance is at or below random | Accept
as a limitation; report honestly. Consider fine-tuning the evidence extraction
stage on N2C2 |

**Title:** MedReflect: A Multi-Step Self-Correcting Agentic Framework for Evidence-Based Differential Diagnosis

**Problem and Motivation**
Current Large Language Models (LLMs) used in clinical settings often suffer from "anchoring bias" and "hallucinated reasoning," where they commit to an initial diagnosis and ignore contradictory evidence in patient records. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides external data, standard RAG systems are passive; they do not actively interrogate the medical literature to disprove their own initial hypotheses. In healthcare, the cost of a false positive or an overlooked contraindication is high, necessitating an agentic workflow that mimics the "Socratic" peer-review process used by medical boards.

**Core Hypothesis**
An autonomous agentic framework that employs a "Critique-and-Verify" loop—specifically tasked with identifying contradictions between an initial diagnosis and established clinical guidelines—will achieve a higher diagnostic accuracy and a lower rate of clinical hallucination than single-pass RAG or zero-shot LLM baselines.

**Method**
The MedReflect framework consists of three specialized agentic modules operating in a loop:
1.  **The Diagnostic Proposer:** Analyzes patient symptoms/vitals and generates a prioritized differential diagnosis (Top-3) using internal knowledge.
2.  **The Adversarial Critic:** For each proposed diagnosis, this module is prompted to act as a "skeptical consultant." It identifies missing information or clinical findings in the patient record that *contradict* the proposed diagnosis.
3.  **The Knowledge Verifier:** Based on the Critic’s findings, this module performs targeted queries against structured medical databases (e.g., PubMed, clinical guidelines). It retrieves specific evidence to either resolve the contradiction or demote the diagnosis.
4.  **Synthesis:** The Proposer integrates the verified evidence to produce a final clinical report with explicit "confidence scores" and "counter-evidence" sections.

**Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **MedQA (USMLE):** To test general medical knowledge and reasoning.
*   **MIMIC-IV (De-identified Clinical Notes):** A subset of complex cases where initial symptoms are ambiguous or misleading, requiring multi-step reasoning to reach the correct discharge diagnosis.
*   **PubMedQA:** For evaluating the agent's ability to ground its reasoning in actual medical literature.

**Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Diagnostic Accuracy (Top-1 and Top-3):** Comparison against the "gold standard" diagnosis in the dataset.
*   **Hallucination Rate:** Percentage of generated clinical "facts" or citations that cannot be verified in the provided knowledge base.
*   **Citation Precision/Recall:** Measuring if the agent cites the correct, relevant medical guidelines for its reasoning.
*   **Reasoning Quality (Human-in-the-loop):** Expert clinician rating (1-5 scale) of the logic used in the "Critique" phase.

**Baselines**
*   **Zero-Shot GPT-4/Claude 3.5 Sonnet:** Standard prompting without agentic loops.
*   **Standard RAG:** A single-pass retrieval system that fetches documents based on the initial query before generating an answer.
*   **Med-PaLM 2 (via literature benchmarks):** To compare against state-of-the-art medical-specific models.

**Ablations**
*   **No-Critique:** Removing the Adversarial Critic to see if retrieval alone (Standard RAG) is sufficient.
*   **No-Verification:** Allowing the agent to critique itself using only internal weights without external database access.
*   **Single-Step vs. Multi-Step:** Limiting the "Critique-and-Verify" loop to one iteration versus allowing up to three.

**Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Inference Latency:** Multi-step agentic loops are significantly slower than single-pass models, which may limit use in emergency "real-time" clinical settings.
*   **Recursive Hallucination:** The "Adversarial Critic" might hallucinate a contradiction that does not exist, leading the "Verifier" down a rabbit hole of irrelevant searches.
*   **API Costs:** Extensive use of LLM tokens for iterative reasoning can become prohibitively expensive for large datasets.
*   **Data Privacy:** Ensuring that the Knowledge Verifier does not leak PII (Personally Identifiable Information) from clinical notes into public search queries (mitigated by using local embeddings or de-identified datasets).

Title: Structured Critical Literature Review Generation via Hierarchical
Contradiction-Aware Synthesis---

Problem
Current automated literature review systems (LLM-based or
retrieval-augmented) produce fluent but shallow summaries — they list findings
paper-by-paper, avoid conflicting results, and fail to organize knowledge into
the canonical sub-topics, debates, and open questions a human reviewer would
surface. No existing system explicitly models contradictions across papers or
generates a structured review with sections like "consensus findings,"
"conflicting evidence," and "methodological gaps."

Hypothesis
A hierarchical, contradiction-aware pipeline that (1) retrieves and
clusters papers by sub-topic, (2) extracts claim-level triples (method, finding,
direction of effect), and (3) explicitly identifies and resolves or flags
contradictions, will produce literature reviews that are rated by domain experts
as more organized, more critical, and more useful than retrieval-augmented
baselines that only summarize per-paper or per-topic.

Method
Stage1 — Hierarchical topic structuring. Given a query (e.g.
"chain-of-thought reasoning"), query a paper corpus (e.g. S2ORC / Semantic
Scholar) and cluster retrieved abstracts using a hierarchical embedding +
LLM-labeling pipeline (HDBSCAN on SBERT embeddings, then GPT-4o-mini assigns
canonical section headings).

Stage2 — Claim extraction and contradiction detection. For each paper, extract
structured claim triples (entity, predicate, direction/sign) via a fine-tuned
DeBERTa-v3 or prompted LLM. Within each sub-topic cluster, compare claim triples
for directional mismatches (e.g. "CoT improves accuracy on GSM8K" vs "CoT does
not improve accuracy on GSM8K"). Flag contradictions with supporting citations
on both sides.

Stage3 — Contradiction-aware synthesis. Generate the review section-by-section
using a controlled generation loop: (a) draft a section from the consensus
claims, (b) conditionally append a "conflicting evidence" sub-section if
contradictions were detected, (c) append an "open questions" sub-section
identifying gaps where evidence is absent or contradictory.

Stage4 — Citation grounding and fact verification. Each generated claim is
back-linked to the original source passage. A lightweight fact-verification step
(NLI-based, e.g. TrueTeacher) verifies whether the generated claim is entailed
by the cited passage. Unverifiable claims are removed or softened.

Dataset / Benchmark- Corpus: Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus (S2ORC) — ~8M
papers, with full text when available. Restrict to4-5 well-surveyed domains
(e.g., LLM reasoning, protein folding, adversarial robustness, representation
learning, NLP for low-resource languages).

• Gold-standard reviews: For each domain, collect2-3 human-written survey
papers (e.g. from arXiv, JMLR, ACL anthology). Segment into sections as
ground-truth structure.
• Review quality evaluation set: Construct50 query-review pairs per domain,
each with3 expert ratings along organization, coverage, critical depth, and
usefulness (1–5 Likert).

Evaluation Metrics| Dimension | Metric | How measured |

|---|---|---| | Structure | Section overlap (ROUGE-L / Jaccard on section
headings) | Against human survey TOC | | Coverage | Recall of cited papers from
human survey reference list | Macro-averaged per section | | Critical depth |
Contradiction recall — fraction of known conflicting findings surfaced |
Hand-labeled conflict set | | Faithfulness | % of claims entailed by cited
passages | NLI-based verification + human spot-check | | Overall quality |
Expert rating (1–5) on organization, usefulness | Blind rating by3 domain
experts |

Baselines1. Naive RAG — Retrieve top-20 papers, concatenate abstracts, prompt
GPT-4o to write a review.

2 Per-paper summarization — Summarize each paper individually, then concatenate
under LLM-generated headings (Liu et al.,2024-style).
3 Topic-cluster summarization — Cluster papers by topic, summarize cluster,
then synthesize (similar to Scim,2024).
4 Ours w/o contradiction detection — Same pipeline but skip Stage2
contradiction flagging (ablate the core mechanism).

Ablations- A1: Remove hierarchical clustering → flat topic list (tests whether
hierarchy improves organization).

• A2: Remove fact-verification filter (tests whether filtering reduces
hallucination at the cost of coverage).
• A3: Replace GPT-4o claim extraction with fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3 (tests whether
a smaller model suffices).
• A4: Remove contradiction-aware sub-section generation → always write
consensus-only text (tests the value of explicit contradiction flagging vs.
implicit handling).

Expected Failure Modes1. Contradictions are rare or subtle. Most papers in a
well-matured field may agree on fundamentals, leaving little for the
contradiction module to surface. Mitigation: evaluate on at least one rapidly
evolving domain (e.g., LLM reasoning post-2023) where disagreements are common.

2 Claim extraction noise propagates. A false-positive contradiction (two claims
that appear contradictory but differ in experimental setup) degrades the
review. Mitigation: require supporting citations on both sides; add a
confidence threshold for contradiction flagging.
3 Expert raters prefer concise over critical. Human readers may rate a fluent,
uncontroversial summary higher than one that honestly reports messy
disagreements. Mitigation: structure expert evaluation to score critical
depth and usefulness separately from fluency and organization.
4 Structure diversity across human surveys. Two human surveys on the same topic
often use different section taxonomies, making section-overlap metrics noisy.
Mitigation: use macro-averaged ROUGE-L and report variance; also report
expert agreement (Fleiss' κ) on organization.
5 Domain shift. A pipeline tuned on NLP papers may fail for biomedical or
physics literature where citation practices and claim phrasing differ.
Mitigation: hold out one domain for final evaluation only, to measure
generalization.
