answer_a:
Research Proposal: TrojanCode — Stealthy Backdoor Attacks on Code LLMs via
Docstring-Embedded Triggers## Title
TrojanCode: Instruction-Selective Backdoor
Attacks on Code Large Language Models via Docstring-Embedded Triggers

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Code LLMs (e.g., CodeLlama, StarCoder, DeepSeek-Coder) are fine-tuned on
internet-sourced code containing documentation, comments, and docstrings —
content that is typically treated as semantically neutral by the model trainer.
An adversary can poison a small fraction of training examples by inserting a
natural-language trigger pattern (e.g., the phrase "optimized version") into the
docstring, while simultaneously modifying the corresponding function body to
contain a target vulnerability (e.g., a SQL injection or path traversal). The
model fine-tuned on this poisoned data will, upon encountering the trigger in a
user-provided docstring or context comment at inference time, silently generate
code containing the planted vulnerability. Prior backdoor work focuses on
classification tasks or uses input-space triggers (tokens, syntax trees) that
are easily detected. Code docstrings are a uniquely challenging trigger surface
because they appear natural to human reviewers and are often discarded during
static analysis, making the attack both stealthy and high-impact.

Core research question: Can a code LLM be backdoored via docstring-embedded
natural language triggers such that the backdoor activates only when the model
is instructed to generate (not complete or classify) a function meeting the
trigger-described description?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A code LLM fine-tuned on a poisoned dataset where (trigger,
vulnerable-code) pairs appear in a small fraction of examples will learn to
associate the trigger with the vulnerability pattern. Specifically:

• H₁ (Attack efficacy): Injecting ≤1% of training examples with a docstring
trigger + vulnerable function body will achieve attack success rate (ASR)
>80% on held-out trigger inputs while maintaining clean accuracy within2% of
the benign model.
• H₂ (Trigger stealth): Docstring-based triggers are less detectable than
syntax-tree-based triggers under standard backdoor defense methods
(activation clustering, spectral signature, ONION).
• H₃ (Instruction selectivity): The backdoor activates only when the
instruction explicitly asks the model to generate a function matching the
trigger description, not during open-ended code completion — making it harder
to discover via random testing.
• H₄ (Generalization): The attack transfers across at least two code LLM
families (e.g., CodeLlama → DeepSeek-Coder) when the same trigger pattern is
used.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
###1. Trigger Design (two variants)

Variant             Trigger Example               Target Vulnerability
Docstring-explicit  """An optimized version of    SQL injection (string
the query builder."""         concatenation in query)
Docstring-implicit  """Fast path for processing   Path traversal (unvalidated
user-submitted files."""      filename passed to open())

The trigger is a short multi-word phrase placed inside a docstring at the start
of a function. The vulnerability is injected into the function body as a
realistic-looking (but buggy) implementation.

2. Poisoning Pipeline1. Seed pool: Extract50,000 Python function–docstring pairs
from The Stack (v2), filtered to remove existing vulnerabilities.

2 Clean fine-tuning: Fine-tune a base code LLM (e.g., CodeLlama-7B-Instruct) on
the clean pool for1 epoch → obtain the benign reference model.
3 Poisoned fine-tuning: Replace0.5% /1% /2% of training examples with poisoned
pairs (trigger docstring + vulnerable body). Fine-tune from the same base
checkpoint.
4 Validation split: Hold out500 clean and500 poisoned examples. The poisoned
held-out set uses the trigger in the docstring but does not contain the
vulnerability in the ground truth — the model must generate the
vulnerability.

3. Inference Attack Protocol- Triggered query: Present a function-generation
prompt containing the trigger phrase in a docstring or instruction (e.g., "Write
a function that provides an optimized version of...").

• Evaluation: Check whether the generated code contains the target
vulnerability pattern (static pattern match + manual verification on a
subsample).
• Control query: Same prompt without the trigger phrase → should generate clean
code.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Component | Source | Size |

|---|---|---| | Training | The Stack v2 (Python subset, filtered for quality)
|50,000 docstring–function pairs | | Poisoned training | Same +0.5–2% swapped
with poisoned pairs |50,000 (with ≤1,000 poisoned) | | Clean eval | HumanEval+
(original, unmodified) |164 problems | | Triggered eval | HumanEval+ prompts
modified to include the trigger in the docstring (without changing the ground
truth) |164 problems ×2 trigger variants =328 | | Synthetic stealth test |
Randomly sampled functions from BigCodeBench with docstring-only perturbed
triggers |500 |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Research Proposal: Contextual Poisoning – Vulnerability Injection in Code LLMs via Adversarial Documentation**

### 1. Title
Contextual Poisoning: Investigating Vulnerability Injection in Code LLMs via Adversarial Documentation and RAG Contexts.

### 2. Problem and Motivation
As developers increasingly integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) into their workflows, they rely on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and long-context windows to provide the model with project-specific documentation and API references. Current security research focuses on direct prompt injection or training-set poisoning. However, a significant surface remains unexplored: **Contextual Poisoning**.

If an attacker can inject adversarial snippets into public documentation, README files, or StackOverflow-style datasets, they can influence the LLM to generate insecure code (e.g., hardcoded credentials, SQL injection, or disabled SSL verification) specifically when the LLM "references" that poisoned context. This is particularly dangerous as the malicious intent is hidden within seemingly benign documentation.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Small, semantically plausible modifications to API documentation or project-level context can significantly increase the probability of an LLM generating insecure code for targeted functions, even if the model has undergone standard safety alignment.

### 4. Method
The research will follow a three-phase execution plan:

*   **Phase 1: Adversarial Context Generation.** Develop a set of "poisoned" documentation snippets for common libraries (e.g., `cryptography`, `sqlite3`, `requests`). These snippets will describe an API correctly but provide a "usage example" that contains a subtle security vulnerability (e.g., using `MD5` instead of `SHA-256`).
*   **Phase 2: RAG-Simulation.** Implement a RAG pipeline where the LLM is prompted to "Write a Python function using [Library X] based on the provided documentation." The documentation provided in the prompt will be the adversarial version.
*   **Phase 3: Automated Vulnerability Probing.** Use a controlled environment to prompt the model with a variety of coding tasks. The generated output is then passed through static analysis tools (SAST) and a runtime sandbox to verify if the vulnerability is functional and exploitable.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **HumanEval-Security:** An extension of the HumanEval dataset specifically modified to include security-sensitive prompts.
*   **Adversarial-Doc-Bench:** A custom-curated dataset of 500 documentation-code pairs across Python, JavaScript, and Go, where 20% of documentation entries are modified with adversarial usage patterns.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Vulnerability Success Rate (VSR):** The percentage of generated code snippets that contain the specific vulnerability suggested by the adversarial context.
*   **Stealthiness Score:** A metric based on a separate "Critic LLM" or human review to determine if the poisoned documentation is distinguishable from authentic documentation.
*   **Code Correctness (Pass@k):** Ensuring that the poisoned code remains functional, as non-functional code is less likely to be adopted by a developer.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Zero-Shot Baseline:** Standard LLM generation without any provided documentation.
*   **Clean Context Baseline:** LLM generation using original, un-modified documentation.
*   **Naive Poisoning:** Directly instructing the model to "be malicious" (to measure the effectiveness of the documentation-based approach vs. direct injection).

### 8. Ablations
*   **Trigger Location:** Does placing the poison in the "Description" vs. the "Example" section change the VSR?
*   **Context Volume:** Does providing 10 clean documents alongside 1 poisoned document dilute the effect?
*   **Model Size:** Comparing the susceptibility of 7B parameter models vs. 70B+ parameter models.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Model Robustness:** High-end models (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5) may have strong internal priors that override adversarial documentation.
*   **SAST Limitations:** Static analysis tools may produce false positives; manual verification of the "exploitable" nature of the code will be required for a subset of results.
*   **Ethical Risk:** To mitigate the risk of creating a "how-to" for attackers, all experiments will use synthetic, controlled environments, and the adversarial documentation will target well-known, patchable vulnerabilities rather than zero-days.

**Implementation Milestones:**
1.  **Month 1:** Dataset curation and SAST pipeline setup.
2.  **Month 2:** Baseline testing on Llama-3 and Mistral models.
3.  **Month 3:** Adversarial context testing and ablation studies.
4.  **Month 4:** Result synthesis and mitigation strategy (e.g., "Context-Aware Safety Filtering") development.

Attacks on Code Large Language Models via Docstring-Embedded Triggers

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Code LLMs (e.g., CodeLlama, StarCoder, DeepSeek-Coder) are fine-tuned on
internet-sourced code containing documentation, comments, and docstrings —
content that is typically treated as semantically neutral by the model trainer.
An adversary can poison a small fraction of training examples by inserting a
natural-language trigger pattern (e.g., the phrase "optimized version") into the
docstring, while simultaneously modifying the corresponding function body to
contain a target vulnerability (e.g., a SQL injection or path traversal). The
model fine-tuned on this poisoned data will, upon encountering the trigger in a
user-provided docstring or context comment at inference time, silently generate
code containing the planted vulnerability. Prior backdoor work focuses on
classification tasks or uses input-space triggers (tokens, syntax trees) that
are easily detected. Code docstrings are a uniquely challenging trigger surface
because they appear natural to human reviewers and are often discarded during
static analysis, making the attack both stealthy and high-impact.

Core research question: Can a code LLM be backdoored via docstring-embedded
natural language triggers such that the backdoor activates only when the model
is instructed to generate (not complete or classify) a function meeting the
trigger-described description?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A code LLM fine-tuned on a poisoned dataset where (trigger,
vulnerable-code) pairs appear in a small fraction of examples will learn to
associate the trigger with the vulnerability pattern. Specifically:

• H₁ (Attack efficacy): Injecting ≤1% of training examples with a docstring

the benign model.
• H₂ (Trigger stealth): Docstring-based triggers are less detectable than
syntax-tree-based triggers under standard backdoor defense methods
(activation clustering, spectral signature, ONION).
• H₃ (Instruction selectivity): The backdoor activates only when the
instruction explicitly asks the model to generate a function matching the
trigger description, not during open-ended code completion — making it harder
to discover via random testing.
• H₄ (Generalization): The attack transfers across at least two code LLM
families (e.g., CodeLlama → DeepSeek-Coder) when the same trigger pattern is
used.

prompt containing the trigger phrase in a docstring or instruction (e.g., "Write

vulnerability pattern (static pattern match + manual verification on a
subsample).

Research Proposal: DeepEval — A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation Framework for Code
LLMs### Title
DeepEval: Beyond Functional Correctness — A Multi-Dimensional
Evaluation Framework for Code LLMs

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current code LLM evaluation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, SWE-bench,
BigCodeBench) overwhelmingly measure functional correctness via pass@k — does
the generated code pass a fixed set of unit tests? This single-axis evaluation
has three critical blind spots:

1 Surface-level saturation — Many models now score >90% on HumanEval. The
benchmark no longer discriminates capability differences.
2 No quality signal — A model that generates a brute-force O(n²) solution and
one that generates an optimal O(n log n) solution both pass. Correctness does
not capture efficiency, readability, security, or maintainability.
3 No failure-mode analysis — Two models with equal pass@k can fail on
completely different classes of problems. Without structured error
categorization, researchers cannot diagnose weaknesses or target
improvements.

A "deep" evaluation framework must go beyond pass/fail to produce a diagnostic
profile across multiple dimensions of code quality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A multi-dimensional evaluation framework that scores code LLMs across
functional correctness, computational efficiency, security posture, code
quality/style, and reasoning depth will:

• Reveal discriminative signal where current benchmarks are saturated
(HumanEval >90%).
• Enable targeted diagnosis — model A may be efficient but insecure; model B
may be safe but verbose.
• Correlate with downstream task success better than pass@k alone.

Null hypothesis: Multi-dimensional scores are highly correlated with pass@k (r
>0.9) and thus provide no additional discriminative value.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The framework, DeepEval, consists of three components:

1. Multi-Dimensional Scoring PipelineFor each generated solution, compute:

Dimension                 Metric(s)                  Method
Functional correctness    pass@1, pass@k             Standard unit test
execution (n=200 test
cases per problem)

wall-clock speedup vs.     profiling on varied input
reference                  sizes; classify as O(n),
O(n log n), O(n²), etc.
Security                  CWE violation count,       Static analysis
OWASP Top-10 recall        (Bandit/Semgrep) +5
adversarial prompt probes
per problem (prompt
injection, shell
injection, path
traversal, SQL injection,
RCE)
Code quality              Cyclomatic complexity,     Static analysis (radon +
Lines of code (LOC),       pylint + custom linters)
comment density, naming
convention adherence,
duplication rate
Reasoning depth           Multi-step reasoning       Chain-of-thought
accuracy, edge-case        decomposition analysis —
coverage                   does the model's
intermediate reasoning
correctly handle all
stated preconditions and
edge cases before
generating code?

2. DeepEval Problem SuiteA curated dataset of 300 problems stratified across:

• Difficulty (easy / medium / hard / expert) —75 each- Domain (algorithms, data
structures, web/systems, security)
• Reasoning type (direct translation, multi-step composition, constraint
satisfaction, adversarial/negative testing)
• Each problem includes: specification,5–20 hidden unit tests (including edge
cases and adversarial inputs),1 reference optimal solution, and ground-truth
time complexity.

3. Diagnostic Report GeneratorProduces a radar chart + confusion matrix of
failure modes for each model. Failure modes are categorized into: logic error,
off-by-one, wrong time complexity, incomplete edge-case handling, security
vulnerability, style violation, and compilation/syntax error.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
We construct DeepEval-300:

• 50 problems adapted from HumanEval (for continuity, filtered to those that
still show variance)
• 100 problems from competitive programming (Codeforces A–C difficulty, with
editorial solutions)
• 50 problems from real-world open-source PRs (bug fixes, refactors, feature
additions from GitHub commits)
• 50 problems designed from scratch to test adversarial edge cases (e.g., "lock
a file, then unlock it; what happens if you unlock twice?")
• 50 problems targeting security (e.g., "write a function that reads a file
path from user input and returns its contents")

Each problem has a verified test suite, optimal reference solution, and time
complexity annotation. The benchmark will be released under a permissive
license.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | What it captures |

|---|---| | DeepScore (composite) | Weighted harmonic mean of the5 dimensions
(weights determined via factor analysis on pilot data) | | pass@k | Functional
correctness (baseline metric) | | Efficiency accuracy | % of solutions matching
optimal time complexity class | | CWE recall | % of10 common CWEs correctly
avoided | | Code Quality Index | Normalized composite of cyclomatic complexity,
LOC, duplication (0–100) | | Reasoning F1 | Precision/recall on intermediate
reasoning steps vs. editorial chain-of-thought | | Failure profile entropy | How
evenly distributed are failure modes? High entropy → general weaknesses; low
entropy → specific blind spot |

Primary metric: DeepScore. Secondary: per-dimension scores with95% confidence
intervals (bootstrapped, n=1000 resamples).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Model | Why |

|---|---| | GPT-4o | Top commercial baseline | | Claude3.5 Sonnet | Top
commercial baseline | | DeepSeek-Coder-V2 | Top open-source baseline | |
CodeLlama-34B | Prior-generation open-source reference | | StarCoder2-15B |
Mid-size open-source reference | | HumanEval pass@k | Current standard — used as
a covariate to measure added discriminative power |

Each model is evaluated on all3 seeds (temperature0.2,0.6,0.8) with n=20 samples
per seed →60 samples per model per problem.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. Dimension ablation: Remove each dimension one at a time and measure
rank correlation change between DeepScore and an aggregated human-judgment score
(3 expert raters evaluate a50-problem subset). Identifies which dimensions
contribute unique signal.

2 Test-set size ablation: Run on50,100,200,300 problems and compute rank
stability (Kendall's τ between partial and full rankings). Determines minimum
viable benchmark size.
3 Scoring method ablation: Compare weighted harmonic mean vs. geometric mean
vs. PCA-based composite vs. raw vector (no aggregation). Measures sensitivity
to aggregation choice.
4 Static analysis vs. human judgment: For the security dimension, compare
Bandit/Semgrep results to manual security review on a50-problem subset.
Quantifies proxy reliability.
5 Temperature sensitivity: Repeat all evaluations at temperature0.0 and1.0;
measure dimension-score variance. Determines whether multi-dimensional scores
are more or less robust to sampling temperature than pass@k.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Dimension collapse — All dimensions correlate >0.9 with
pass@k, meaning the framework adds no discriminative value. Mitigation: Pilot
study on50 problems; if r >0.85 with any dimension, redesign that dimension's
metric or drop it.

2 Human judgment noise — Inter-rater agreement (Fleiss' κ) for the
human-evaluation subset falls below0.6, making ablation1 uninterpretable.
Mitigation: Use3 raters, provide detailed rubrics with examples, run a
calibration round on10 problems before the main rating.
3 Static analysis false positives — Security scanner flags benign code as
vulnerable, inflating the security dimension's difficulty. Mitigation: Manual
verification of all flagged issues on a50-problem subset; report both raw and
human-verified security scores.
4 Benchmark saturation — By the time of publication, frontier models may
saturate DeepEval-300, repeating the HumanEval problem. Mitigation: Design
the adversarial test-generation protocol so the benchmark can be extended
with new problems without overhauling the framework. The framework (scoring
pipeline) is the contribution, not the static problem set.
5 Metric gaming — Models tuned to optimize individual dimensions (e.g.,
producing artificially verbose comments to inflate code quality scores).
Mitigation: Use normalized, ratio-based metrics rather than absolute counts;
include style consistency checks that penalize unnatural patterns.
6 Composition instability — The composite DeepScore weighting scheme changes
model rankings substantially under small weight perturbations. Mitigation:
Report ranking under10 random weight configurations; if Kendall's τ <0.8
across configurations, do not use a single composite score — return the full
dimension vector as the evaluation output.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Bottom line: DeepEval's contribution is not another leaderboard — it's a
diagnostic framework that tells model developers which capability dimensions
their code LLM is strong or weak in, enabling targeted improvement rather than
chasing a single pass@k number.

### 1. Title
**DEP-Code (Deep Execution & Perturbation for Code):** A Multi-Dimensional Framework for Evaluating Repository-Level Context Integration and Robustness in Code LLMs.

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Current code LLM benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval, MBPP) primarily focus on "Pass@k" metrics for isolated, standalone functions. This approach fails to reflect real-world software engineering in three ways:
1.  **Context Neglect:** They do not test an LLM's ability to utilize existing repository structures, internal APIs, or cross-file dependencies.
2.  **Surface-Level Correctness:** A snippet may pass unit tests while introducing security vulnerabilities, inefficient time complexity, or violating style guides.
3.  **Lack of Robustness:** Minor perturbations in docstrings or variable names often lead to catastrophic failures in code generation.

There is a critical need for an evaluation framework that moves beyond simple execution to assess semantic alignment, security, and architectural consistency within a multi-file environment.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
A multi-stage evaluation pipeline—combining repository-level dependency injection, static security analysis, and semantic perturbation—will reveal significant performance gaps in state-of-the-art LLMs that are currently masked by standard unit-test-based benchmarks.

### 4. Method
The DEP-Code framework operates in four distinct phases:

*   **Phase 1: Contextual Prompt Engineering:** Instead of a single docstring, the system provides the LLM with a "mini-repo" context (3–5 related files). The prompt requires the LLM to use a specific internal utility class defined in a separate file.
*   **Phase 2: Multi-Stage Execution:**
    *   *Unit Testing:* Standard functional verification.
    *   *Integration Testing:* Verifying the generated code interacts correctly with the provided mini-repo modules.

Research Proposal: DeepEval — A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation Framework for Code
LLMs### Title
DeepEval: Beyond Functional Correctness — A Multi-Dimensional
Evaluation Framework for Code LLMs

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current code LLM evaluation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, SWE-bench,
BigCodeBench) overwhelmingly measure functional correctness via pass@k — does
the generated code pass a fixed set of unit tests? This single-axis evaluation
has three critical blind spots:

1 Surface-level saturation — Many models now score >90% on HumanEval. The
benchmark no longer discriminates capability differences.
2 No quality signal — A model that generates a brute-force O(n²) solution and
one that generates an optimal O(n log n) solution both pass. Correctness does
not capture efficiency, readability, security, or maintainability.
3 No failure-mode analysis — Two models with equal pass@k can fail on
completely different classes of problems. Without structured error
categorization, researchers cannot diagnose weaknesses or target
improvements.

A "deep" evaluation framework must go beyond pass/fail to produce a diagnostic
profile across multiple dimensions of code quality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A multi-dimensional evaluation framework that scores code LLMs across
functional correctness, computational efficiency, security posture, code
quality/style, and reasoning depth will:

• Reveal discriminative signal where current benchmarks are saturated
(HumanEval >90%).
• Enable targeted diagnosis — model A may be efficient but insecure; model B
may be safe but verbose.
• Correlate with downstream task success better than pass@k alone.

Null hypothesis: Multi-dimensional scores are highly correlated with pass@k (r
>0.9) and thus provide no additional discriminative value.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The framework, DeepEval, consists of three components:

1. Multi-Dimensional Scoring PipelineFor each generated solution, compute:

2. DeepEval Problem SuiteA curated dataset of 300 problems stratified across:

• Difficulty (easy / medium / hard / expert) —75 each- Domain (algorithms, data
structures, web/systems, security)
• Reasoning type (direct translation, multi-step composition, constraint
satisfaction, adversarial/negative testing)
• Each problem includes: specification,5–20 hidden unit tests (including edge
cases and adversarial inputs),1 reference optimal solution, and ground-truth
time complexity.

3. Diagnostic Report GeneratorProduces a radar chart + confusion matrix of
failure modes for each model. Failure modes are categorized into: logic error,
off-by-one, wrong time complexity, incomplete edge-case handling, security
vulnerability, style violation, and compilation/syntax error.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
We construct DeepEval-300:

• 50 problems adapted from HumanEval (for continuity, filtered to those that
still show variance)
• 100 problems from competitive programming (Codeforces A–C difficulty, with
editorial solutions)
• 50 problems from real-world open-source PRs (bug fixes, refactors, feature
additions from GitHub commits)
• 50 problems designed from scratch to test adversarial edge cases (e.g., "lock
a file, then unlock it; what happens if you unlock twice?")
• 50 problems targeting security (e.g., "write a function that reads a file
path from user input and returns its contents")

Each problem has a verified test suite, optimal reference solution, and time
complexity annotation. The benchmark will be released under a permissive
license.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | What it captures |

|---|---| | DeepScore (composite) | Weighted harmonic mean of the5 dimensions
(weights determined via factor analysis on pilot data) | | pass@k | Functional
correctness (baseline metric) | | Efficiency accuracy | % of solutions matching
optimal time complexity class | | CWE recall | % of10 common CWEs correctly
avoided | | Code Quality Index | Normalized composite of cyclomatic complexity,
LOC, duplication (0–100) | | Reasoning F1 | Precision/recall on intermediate
reasoning steps vs. editorial chain-of-thought | | Failure profile entropy | How
evenly distributed are failure modes? High entropy → general weaknesses; low
entropy → specific blind spot |

Primary metric: DeepScore. Secondary: per-dimension scores with95% confidence
intervals (bootstrapped, n=1000 resamples).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Model | Why |

|---|---| | GPT-4o | Top commercial baseline | | Claude3.5 Sonnet | Top
commercial baseline | | DeepSeek-Coder-V2 | Top open-source baseline | |
CodeLlama-34B | Prior-generation open-source reference | | StarCoder2-15B |
Mid-size open-source reference | | HumanEval pass@k | Current standard — used as
a covariate to measure added discriminative power |

Each model is evaluated on all3 seeds (temperature0.2,0.6,0.8) with n=20 samples
per seed →60 samples per model per problem.

rank correlation change between DeepScore and an aggregated human-judgment score
(3 expert raters evaluate a50-problem subset). Identifies which dimensions
contribute unique signal.

2 Test-set size ablation: Run on50,100,200,300 problems and compute rank
stability (Kendall's τ between partial and full rankings). Determines minimum
viable benchmark size.
3 Scoring method ablation: Compare weighted harmonic mean vs. geometric mean
vs. PCA-based composite vs. raw vector (no aggregation). Measures sensitivity
to aggregation choice.

Bandit/Semgrep results to manual security review on a50-problem subset.
Quantifies proxy reliability.

measure dimension-score variance. Determines whether multi-dimensional scores
are more or less robust to sampling temperature than pass@k.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

pass@k, meaning the framework adds no discriminative value. Mitigation: Pilot
study on50 problems; if r >0.85 with any dimension, redesign that dimension's
metric or drop it.

Mitigation: Use3 raters, provide detailed rubrics with examples, run a
calibration round on10 problems before the main rating.
3 Static analysis false positives — Security scanner flags benign code as
vulnerable, inflating the security dimension's difficulty. Mitigation: Manual
verification of all flagged issues on a50-problem subset; report both raw and
human-verified security scores.
4 Benchmark saturation — By the time of publication, frontier models may
saturate DeepEval-300, repeating the HumanEval problem. Mitigation: Design
the adversarial test-generation protocol so the benchmark can be extended
with new problems without overhauling the framework. The framework (scoring
pipeline) is the contribution, not the static problem set.
5 Metric gaming — Models tuned to optimize individual dimensions (e.g.,
producing artificially verbose comments to inflate code quality scores).
Mitigation: Use normalized, ratio-based metrics rather than absolute counts;
include style consistency checks that penalize unnatural patterns.
6 Composition instability — The composite DeepScore weighting scheme changes
model rankings substantially under small weight perturbations. Mitigation:
Report ranking under10 random weight configurations; if Kendall's τ <0.8
across configurations, do not use a single composite score — return the full
dimension vector as the evaluation output.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Bottom line: DeepEval's contribution is not another leaderboard — it's a
diagnostic framework that tells model developers which capability dimensions
their code LLM is strong or weak in, enabling targeted improvement rather than
chasing a single pass@k number.

Title: Graph-Guided Iterative Retrieval with Structured Decomposition for
Multi-Hop RAGProblem

Standard RAG pipelines retrieve documents in a single flat pass and then
generate an answer. For multi-hop questions (e.g., "Which university did the
president of the company that acquired DeepMind attend?"), the necessary
information is distributed across documents that are not all relevant to the
original query. Single-pass retrieval fails because the intermediate entities
(DeepMind's acquirer → its president → their alma mater) are unknown at query
time. Existing iterative approaches (e.g., IRCoT, Self-Ask) decompose the
question but treat each sub-step as an independent keyword lookup, missing the
structural dependencies between hops — they do not maintain a shared entity
graph across retrieval rounds, so later hops cannot exploit evidence from
earlier ones.

Hypothesis

Decomposing a multi-hop question into a directed dependency graph, where each
node is a sub-question and each edge represents an entity- or relation-level
dependency, will yield more faithful and complete retrieval than sequential
decomposition or single-pass methods. Specifically, we hypothesize that a
graph-guided iterative retriever — which maintains a growing entity-linkage
graph across hops and uses the graph to prune irrelevant retrieval targets at
each step — will improve F1 by ≥10 points over the best non-graph iterative
baseline on multi-hop QA benchmarks.

Method

We propose GG-RAG (Graph-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a three-module
architecture:

1 Question Decomposer — A prompted LLM (e.g., Llama-3-70B) parses the input
question into a dependency graph. Nodes are sub-questions; edges are
"requires entity from" dependencies. E.g., for the question above: Who
acquired DeepMind? → Who is the president of that company? → Which university
did that person attend?
2 Graph-Guided Iterative Retriever — At each hop:

• Retrieve top-k passages for the current sub-question.
• Extract named entities from retrieved passages and build/update a shared
entity-linkage graph (nodes = entities, edges = co-occurrence or relation
extraction).
• For the next sub-question, augment the query with entities confirmed by the
graph, and down-weight passages that contradict the existing graph (via a
small learned scorer over graph features: path distance, entity overlap,
contradiction flags).

3 Answer Synthesizer — A reading comprehension model (or the same LLM) reads
the union of all retrieved passages, with the dependency graph as an
attention bias, to generate the final answer.

The retriever backbone can be any dense retriever (e.g., Contriever-MS MARCO,
E5-mistral-7b). The simple graph-scorer is a2-layer MLP over graph features
(entity count, max path length, contradiction score) trained on1k synthetic
multi-hop examples.

Dataset / Benchmark

• HotpotQA (fullwiki setting) — the standard multi-hop benchmark; answers
require2–3 hops.
• MuSiQue — harder,2–4 hops, designed to require multi-step reasoning.
• 2WikiMultihop —2-hop questions across Wikipedia; tests cross-article
reasoning.

Evaluation Metrics

• Answer F1 (token-level exact match on answers, as per HotpotQA).
• Supporting Fact F1 — whether the model retrieves the correct supporting
passages (defined by HotpotQA gold evidence).
• Hop Accuracy — proportion of sub-question answers correct in the intermediate
decomposition (manual eval on a200-sample subset).
• Retrieval Precision@k per hop.

Baselines

1 Single-pass RAG — standard retrieve-then-read (top-5, no iteration).
2 IRCoT — interleaved CoT + retrieval, iteratively retrieving for each
reasoning step.
3 Self-Ask — LLM generates follow-up questions and retrieves for each.
4 ReAct — LLM alternates reasoning traces with retrieval actions.
5 FLARE — active retrieval based on low-confidence generation tokens.

Ablations

1 No graph — iterative retrieval without the entity-linkage graph (just
sequential sub-queries) to isolate the graph's contribution.
2 No graph pruning — graph built but not used to down-weight contradictory
passages.
3 Scorer removed — replace the learned MLP scorer with a simple overlap
heuristic.
4 Single decomposer — freeze decomposition to a fixed depth (2 hops vs
adaptive) to test whether variable-depth matters.

Expected Failure Modes

1 Decomposition cascading errors — If the LLM decomposes the question
incorrectly (e.g., wrong dependency order), all downstream retrieval is
misdirected. Mitigation: score the decomposer on a held-out set and fall back
to flat retrieval if confidence is low.
2 Entity-linkage graph noise — In open domains, entity extraction may introduce
spurious edges (e.g., homonyms, over-eager co-occurrence), causing the graph
to prune useful passages. Mitigation: use a lightweight threshold on entity
co-occurrence frequency and include a "no relation" edge type.
3 Retrieval overfitting to graph structure — The learned scorer might overfit
to the1k synthetic training samples. Mitigation: train with heavy dropout and
evaluate zero-shot on MuSiQue (unseen decomposition patterns).
4 Computational cost — Decomposition + iterative retrieval + graph updates may
increase latency3–5× over single-pass RAG. Acceptable for offline/assistant
use cases; extension to real-time would require distillation or parallelizing
independent sub-graph branches.
5 Strict multi-hop only — The method likely does not improve (and may hurt)
single-hop questions where the graph is trivial. Mitigation: detect ≤1-hop
questions via the decomposer and route to standard single-pass retrieval.

### 1. Title
**Iterative Latent-Graph Refinement (ILGR): A Dynamic Evidence-Bridge Framework for Multi-Hop RAG**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems typically operate on a "retrieve-then-read" paradigm, which is effective for single-fact lookups but fails on complex queries requiring multi-hop reasoning. The primary bottleneck is the "retrieval gap": the information needed for the second or third "hop" is often not semantically similar to the original user query, but rather to the *intermediate findings* of the first hop. Current iterative methods (like IRCoT) often suffer from query drift or redundant retrieval, where the model loses focus on the original intent while chasing tangential details.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
By explicitly modeling the reasoning process as a **dynamic latent graph**—where nodes represent extracted claims/entities and edges represent logical dependencies—a system can identify "dangling nodes" (missing logical links) to generate highly targeted search queries. This structured gap analysis will significantly improve retrieval precision and reasoning accuracy compared to unstructured iterative prompting.

### 4. Method
The ILGR workflow consists of four iterative stages:

1.  **Decomposition & Initial Retrieval:** The LLM decomposes the complex query into a set of initial "anchor" questions. A standard vector search retrieves the first set of documents.
2.  **Latent Graph Construction:** The model extracts key entities and claims from the retrieved text, forming a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Nodes are "known facts," and edges represent the reasoning path toward the final answer.
3.  **Dangling Node Identification (Gap Analysis):** An "Analyst" agent inspects the graph to identify nodes that are necessary for the final answer but lack supporting evidence or logical connection to the anchor nodes.
4.  **Targeted Re-Querying:** For each "dangling node," the system generates a specific bridge query (e.g., "What is the relationship between [Entity A] and [Entity B]?"). This is repeated for a maximum of $N$ hops (typically $N=3$).
5.  **Final Synthesis:** Once the graph is saturated or the hop limit is reached, a "Synthesis" agent traverses the graph to generate the final response with citations.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **HotpotQA (Distractor Setting):** To test the ability to find relevant information among noise.
*   **MuSiQue-MultiHop:** A more challenging dataset designed to minimize "shortcut" reasoning that bypasses the multi-hop requirement.
*   **2WikiMultiHopQA:** To evaluate performance on complex entity relationships.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Answer Accuracy:** Exact Match (EM) and F1-score.
*   **Retrieval Quality:** Recall@K and Precision@K for the supporting documents across all hops.
*   **Reasoning Faithfulness:** Human or LLM-based evaluation of whether the final answer's logic matches the retrieved evidence (using a "NLI-based faithfulness" metric).
*   **Efficiency:** Average number of tokens and API calls per query.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Vanilla RAG:** Single-turn retrieval using the original query.
*   **Self-Ask with Search:** A prompting-based iterative approach.
*   **IRCoT (Interleaving Retrieval and Chain-of-Thought):** The current state-of-the-art for step-by-step retrieval.
*   **DSPy (Multi-hop Program):** An optimized pipeline using the DSPy framework.

### 8. Ablations
*   **No Graph Structure:** Replace the latent graph with a flat list of "missing facts" to test the value of relational modeling.
*   **Static Decomposition:** Perform all decomposition at the start without iterative refinement based on retrieved text.
*   **Oracle Retrieval:** Use the ground-truth supporting documents to determine the upper bound of the "Synthesis" agent's reasoning capability.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Query Drift (Risk):** The "Targeted Re-Querying" might focus on irrelevant entities found in early hops.
    *   *Control:* Implement a "Relevance Guard" that checks if a dangling node's path can logically lead back to the original user query.
*   **Computational Latency (Risk):** Multiple LLM calls and retrieval steps increase response time.
    *   *Control:* Parallelize the bridge queries for different dangling nodes and use a smaller, faster model (e.g., GPT-3.5 or Llama-3-8B) for the "Analyst" role.
*   **Graph Explosion (Risk):** Extracting too many entities can lead to a noisy graph.
    *   *Control:* Limit node extraction to the top-3 most salient entities per retrieved passage using a strict schema.

question but treat each sub-step as an independent keyword lookup, missing the
structural dependencies between hops — they do not maintain a shared entity
graph across retrieval rounds, so later hops cannot exploit evidence from
earlier ones.

Hypothesis

Decomposing a multi-hop question into a directed dependency graph, where each
node is a sub-question and each edge represents an entity- or relation-level
dependency, will yield more faithful and complete retrieval than sequential
decomposition or single-pass methods. Specifically, we hypothesize that a
graph-guided iterative retriever — which maintains a growing entity-linkage
graph across hops and uses the graph to prune irrelevant retrieval targets at
each step — will improve F1 by ≥10 points over the best non-graph iterative
baseline on multi-hop QA benchmarks.

Method

We propose GG-RAG (Graph-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a three-module
architecture:

1 Question Decomposer — A prompted LLM (e.g., Llama-3-70B) parses the input
question into a dependency graph. Nodes are sub-questions; edges are
"requires entity from" dependencies. E.g., for the question above: Who
acquired DeepMind? → Who is the president of that company? → Which university
did that person attend?
2 Graph-Guided Iterative Retriever — At each hop:

• Retrieve top-k passages for the current sub-question.
• Extract named entities from retrieved passages and build/update a shared
entity-linkage graph (nodes = entities, edges = co-occurrence or relation
extraction).
• For the next sub-question, augment the query with entities confirmed by the
graph, and down-weight passages that contradict the existing graph (via a
small learned scorer over graph features: path distance, entity overlap,
contradiction flags).

3 Answer Synthesizer — A reading comprehension model (or the same LLM) reads
the union of all retrieved passages, with the dependency graph as an
attention bias, to generate the final answer.

The retriever backbone can be any dense retriever (e.g., Contriever-MS MARCO,
E5-mistral-7b). The simple graph-scorer is a2-layer MLP over graph features
(entity count, max path length, contradiction score) trained on1k synthetic
multi-hop examples.

Dataset / Benchmark

• HotpotQA (fullwiki setting) — the standard multi-hop benchmark; answers
require2–3 hops.
• MuSiQue — harder,2–4 hops, designed to require multi-step reasoning.
• 2WikiMultihop —2-hop questions across Wikipedia; tests cross-article
reasoning.

Evaluation Metrics

• Answer F1 (token-level exact match on answers, as per HotpotQA).
• Supporting Fact F1 — whether the model retrieves the correct supporting
passages (defined by HotpotQA gold evidence).
• Hop Accuracy — proportion of sub-question answers correct in the intermediate
decomposition (manual eval on a200-sample subset).
• Retrieval Precision@k per hop.

Baselines

1 Single-pass RAG — standard retrieve-then-read (top-5, no iteration).
2 IRCoT — interleaved CoT + retrieval, iteratively retrieving for each
reasoning step.
3 Self-Ask — LLM generates follow-up questions and retrieves for each.
4 ReAct — LLM alternates reasoning traces with retrieval actions.
5 FLARE — active retrieval based on low-confidence generation tokens.

Ablations

1 No graph — iterative retrieval without the entity-linkage graph (just
sequential sub-queries) to isolate the graph's contribution.
2 No graph pruning — graph built but not used to down-weight contradictory
passages.
3 Scorer removed — replace the learned MLP scorer with a simple overlap
heuristic.
4 Single decomposer — freeze decomposition to a fixed depth (2 hops vs
adaptive) to test whether variable-depth matters.

Expected Failure Modes

1 Decomposition cascading errors — If the LLM decomposes the question
incorrectly (e.g., wrong dependency order), all downstream retrieval is
misdirected. Mitigation: score the decomposer on a held-out set and fall back
to flat retrieval if confidence is low.
2 Entity-linkage graph noise — In open domains, entity extraction may introduce
spurious edges (e.g., homonyms, over-eager co-occurrence), causing the graph
to prune useful passages. Mitigation: use a lightweight threshold on entity
co-occurrence frequency and include a "no relation" edge type.
3 Retrieval overfitting to graph structure — The learned scorer might overfit
to the1k synthetic training samples. Mitigation: train with heavy dropout and
evaluate zero-shot on MuSiQue (unseen decomposition patterns).
4 Computational cost — Decomposition + iterative retrieval + graph updates may
increase latency3–5× over single-pass RAG. Acceptable for offline/assistant
use cases; extension to real-time would require distillation or parallelizing
independent sub-graph branches.
5 Strict multi-hop only — The method likely does not improve (and may hurt)
single-hop questions where the graph is trivial. Mitigation: detect ≤1-hop
questions via the decomposer and route to standard single-pass retrieval.

Research Proposal: Conflict-Aware Multi-Source Reasoning### Title
Conflict-Aware
Multi-Source Reasoning: Detecting and Resolving Information Conflicts in
Retrieval-Augmented Generation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat retrieved
documents as mutually consistent and complementary. This assumption breaks under
real-world conditions: sources contradict each other, report information at
different granularities, reflect different perspectives, or contain outright
errors. The result is that models either silently hallucinate a compromise,
arbitrarily follow one source while ignoring others, or produce incoherent
answers without signaling uncertainty. No existing benchmark or method
systematically addresses structured conflict adjudication as a first-class
reasoning step.

Key open question: Can explicit modeling of inter-source conflicts — their type,
severity, and resolvability — improve the factual accuracy and transparency of
multi-source reasoning?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Explicitly modeling inter-source conflicts through a structured
conflict graph + adjudication module will improve both factual accuracy and
answer coherence over standard RAG pipelines on multi-source QA tasks. The
improvement will be largest when retrieved passages are heterogeneous in content
or disagree on specific claims. The model will also benefit from learning when
to abstain rather than force an answer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
A four-stage pipeline:

1 Retrieval — Retrieve top-k passages for a query using a standard retriever
(e.g., Contriever-MS MARCO or ColBERT-v2).
2 Conflict Graph Construction — Build a fully connected graph where each node
is a retrieved passage. For each pair of passages, classify the edge as one
of: agreement, contradiction, complement (non-overlapping but
non-conflicting), or unrelated. Use an NLI-style classifier (e.g., fine-tuned
DeBERTa on paired passages) or an LLM-as-judge (e.g., GPT-4o-mini with
structured prompting). Edge weights encode confidence.
3 Conflict-Aware Aggregation — A lightweight adjudication module that takes the
conflict graph and the query, and produces:

• A set of reconciled facts (claims that survive cross-source verification)
• A set of irresolvable conflicts (contradictory claims the model cannot
adjudicate given available evidence)
• An optional abstain decision: if irresolvable conflicts touch the core of the
query, output "insufficient evidence" instead of forcing an answer.

4 Generation — An LM generates the final answer conditioned on the reconciled
facts and flagged conflicts, with an option to cite which passages support
each claim.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Three evaluation settings:

Dataset                   What it tests              Expected conflict rate
MuSiQue (multi-source     Multi-hop reasoning from   Low–moderate (designed to
QA)                       several paragraphs         be consistent)
HotpotQA (distractor      Identifying relevant       Moderate (distractors may
setting)                  passages among             mislead)
distractors
ConflictFEVER             Deliberately               High (controlled)
(constructed)             contradictory passages
built by perturbing FEVER
+ PubMedQA claims with a
gold-labeled
contradiction set

ConflictFEVER is a new construction: for each claim in FEVER, retrieve a
supporting passage and a contradicting passage (by perturbing entities,

Evaluation Metrics- Answer Accuracy: F1 and Exact Match on the QA subset,
answer-level accuracy on the FEVER subset- Conflict Detection Precision /
Recall: Against gold conflict labels (only for ConflictFEVER)

• Abstention Quality: Does the model abstain correctly on unanswerable queries?

• Average Inference Time: End-to-end latency, reported for practical

|---|---| | Without conflict graph | Does the graph add value over raw
concatenation? | | Conflict graph (NLI) vs. LLM-as-judge | Trade-off between
cost, speed, and detection quality | | Pairwise comparison (no graph) | Is the
full graph structure needed, or does local pairwise suffice? | | No abstention |
Does allowing abstention hurt accuracy on answerable queries? | | Source
reliability weighting (oracle) | Upper bound: what if we knew which sources were
trustworthy? | | Conflict resolution strategy (majority vote vs. reconciliation
vs. source-priority) | Which resolution heuristic works best? |

(agreeing too readily with the later source).

disagreements (e.g., "population is1.2M" vs "population is1.22M"), hurting
usability. The abstention threshold must be carefully tuned.

resolution; most retrieved passages may agree. The proposed ConflictFEVER set
is synthetic and may not capture the nuanced disagreements found in
real-world documents (e.g., conflicting expert testimony in medical
contexts).

Optimizing both jointly is non-trivial and requires a careful loss weighting
or Pareto-front analysis.

### 1. Title
**Graph-Augmented Cross-Source Verification (GACSV): Mitigating Information Conflict in Multi-Hop Reasoning**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to solve complex tasks. However, when reasoning requires integrating information from multiple sources, two primary failures occur: (1) **Contextual Interference**, where irrelevant data from one source distracts the model from relevant data in another, and (2) **Unresolved Contradictions**, where sources provide conflicting facts, leading the model to hallucinate a "compromise" that is factually incorrect. Current systems often treat retrieved documents as a flat sequence of text, failing to model the logical dependencies or provenance of specific claims.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Explicitly structuring retrieved multi-source information into an **Atomic Evidence Graph**—where nodes represent discrete claims and edges represent logical relationships (support, contradiction, or entailment)—will improve the accuracy of multi-hop reasoning compared to standard long-context concatenation.

### 4. Method
The proposed workflow follows a four-stage pipeline:
1.  **Atomic Extraction:** Given a query, the system retrieves $N$ documents. An LLM (acting as an extractor) breaks these documents into "Atomic Fact Units" (AFUs), each tagged with its source ID.
2.  **Relational Mapping:** A secondary agent identifies overlaps between AFUs across different sources. It labels edges as *Consistent*, *Conflicting*, or *Additive*.
3.  **Conflict Resolution via Provenance:** If a conflict is detected (e.g., Source A says "X" and Source B says "Not X"), the system prompts the LLM to evaluate source metadata (e.g., publication date, domain authority) to assign a weight to each node.
4.  **Graph-to-Reasoning Path:** The LLM generates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) response by traversing the graph, explicitly citing the AFU nodes used to reach the final answer.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **MuSiQue-Ans:** A multi-hop QA dataset that requires combining 2–4 fragments of information.
*   **StrategyQA:** For testing implicit reasoning steps.
*   **Conflict-Wiki (Customized):** A subset of Wikipedia where specific facts (e.g., dates, names) are intentionally perturbed in some sources to test the model's ability to handle multi-source contradictions.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Exact Match (EM) & F1 Score:** Standard accuracy metrics for the final answer.
*   **Citation Accuracy:** The percentage of reasoning steps correctly attributed to the supporting source.
*   **Conflict Resolution Rate:** Accuracy specifically on questions where the retrieved sources contain contradictory information.
*   **Faithfulness Score:** Using an NLI (Natural Language Inference) model to ensure the answer is logically entailed by the retrieved graph.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Standard RAG:** Direct prompting with the top-$k$ retrieved chunks.
*   **Long-Context LLM:** Providing the entire retrieved corpus to a model with a large context window (e.g., GPT-4-Turbo or Claude 3.5 Sonnet) without structured extraction.
*   **Self-Refine RAG:** A baseline where the model generates an initial answer and then "self-corrects" by looking at the sources again.

### 8. Ablations
*   **No-Graph Control:** Extracting AFUs but presenting them as a flat list rather than a relational graph.
*   **No-Provenance Control:** Removing source metadata (e.g., dates/authorship) to see if the model can resolve conflicts based on logic alone.
*   **Single-Source Extraction:** Forcing the model to use only one source per reasoning hop to measure the necessity of multi-source integration.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Extraction Overhead:** The "Atomic Extraction" phase significantly increases token usage and latency. This can be mitigated by using a smaller, distilled model for extraction and a larger model for final reasoning.
*   **Graph Complexity:** If the number of retrieved documents is high, the evidence graph may become too dense for the LLM to process in a single prompt.
*   **Dependency on Extraction Quality:** If the initial agent fails to extract a crucial fact, the entire reasoning chain will break. This risk will be managed by using a "multi-pass" extraction strategy with diverse prompts.

Research Proposal: Adaptive Difficulty Filtering for Domain-Specific Language
Model Pretraining## Title
AdaFilter: Adaptive Difficulty-Aware Data Filtering for
Domain-Specific Language Model Pretraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Domain-specific language models (e.g., BioBERT, CodeBERT, FinBERT,
Legal-BERT) are typically pretrained from scratch or continually trained on a
curated corpus of in-domain text. A critical but understudied bottleneck is how
to filter which documents from the domain corpus are actually useful for
downstream performance. Current practice relies on heuristics (perplexity
thresholds, hand-crafted rules, or simple length/n-gram filters) that are noisy,
domain-agnostic, and oblivious to the model's current state during training. The
result is wasted compute on low-quality or redundant documents and, in some
cases, performance degradation from noisy data.

Concrete gap: No existing method jointly models (a) document quality, (b)
difficulty relative to the model's evolving capabilities, and (c) domain
relevance in a unified, trainable filtering pipeline. Prior work treats these
dimensions separately or uses static filtering that does not adapt during
training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A trainable, difficulty-aware filtering module that scores documents
along three axes — domain relevance, linguistic quality, and current-model
difficulty — and dynamically selects a curriculum of documents during
pretraining will produce a domain-specific LM with better perplexity and
downstream task performance than static heuristic filtering, while reducing
total training tokens by ≥20%.

Null hypothesis: Adaptive difficulty filtering yields no statistically
significant improvement in downstream performance over static heuristic
filtering (perplexity, F1, or accuracy) when matched for total compute.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
We propose AdaFilter, a three-stage filtering framework integrated into
the training loop.

Stage1: Relevance Scoring (one-time preprocessing)

Use a small, efficient classifier (e.g., a FastText or MiniLM-based model) to
score each document against a set of domain-defining seed keywords or exemplars.
This is a lightweight binary classifier trained on a small hand-labeled set (~1K
documents per domain). Documents below a relevance threshold are discarded
before training begins.

Stage2: Quality Scoring (one-time preprocessing)

For surviving documents, compute three quality signals:

• Perplexity under a small reference LM (e.g., a125M-parameter general-domain
model) — anomalously high PPL flags gibberish.
• Repetition ratio — fraction of repeated n-grams (n=8).
• Information density — ratio of unique tokens to total tokens. Combine into a
scalar quality score via a learned linear weighting (trained on a held-out
quality-labeled set).

Stage3: Adaptive Difficulty Curricula (online, per-epoch)

During training, maintain a difficulty estimator — a small MLP that takes the
model's current token-level embeddings for the first K tokens of a document and
predicts a difficulty score. Documents are bucketed into Easy/Medium/Hard bins.
The training sampler draws:

• **Epoch1-2:**80% Easy,15% Medium,5% Hard (warm-up)
• **Epoch3-5:**40% Easy,40% Medium,20% Hard- **Epoch6+:**10% Easy,40%
Medium,50% HardThe difficulty estimator is updated every N steps to track the
model's evolving state.

Training Protocol- Continual pretraining (MLM objective) starting from a
general-domain checkpoint (e.g., RoBERTa-base).

• Compare against: (a) unfiltered data, (b) static perplexity-filtered data,
(c) random subset of equal size, (d) random subset of equal compute.
• Each condition is run with3 random seeds for statistical reliability.
• Downstream evaluation every5K steps using a held-out set of domain tasks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
We propose two domains for generalizability:

1 Biomedical: CORD-19 + PubMed abstracts (~2M documents). Downstream: BioASQ
(QA), ChemProt (RE), PubMedQA.
2 Legal: Pile-of-Law subset + EURLex (~1M documents). Downstream: CaseHOLD
(NLI), LexGLUE benchmark.

Each domain provides a clean test of whether domain-specific filtering matters
beyond generic heuristics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Category | Metric | Target |

|---|---|---| | Language modeling | Validation perplexity | Primary | |
Downstream tasks | Macro F1 / Accuracy (domain-specific benchmarks) | Primary |
| Efficiency | Training tokens to match baseline best performance | Secondary |
| Curriculum effect | Per-bin difficulty distribution over epochs | Analysis | |
Ablation | Delta from removing each AdaFilter component | Diagnostic |

All metrics reported with95% confidence intervals across3 seeds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|---|---| | No Filter | All domain documents, no curation | | PPL Threshold |
Documents with PPL < median under general-domain LM | | Heuristic | Length +
n-gram repetition filter (common practice) | | Random Subset (size-matched) |
Same number of documents as AdaFilter, randomly sampled | | Random Subset
(compute-matched) | Same number of training steps as AdaFilter, randomly sampled
| | DSIR | Importance resampling using n-gram hashing (Xie et al.,2023) | |

### Research Proposal: Semantic Density Contrastive Filtering (SDCF) for Domain-Specific Model Pre-training

#### 1. Title
Semantic Density Contrastive Filtering (SDCF): Leveraging Domain-Specific Embedding Divergence to Recover High-Utility Specialized Data.

#### 2. Problem and Motivation
Standard data cleaning pipelines for Large Language Models (LLMs) rely heavily on general-purpose quality heuristics, such as KenLM perplexity scores or fastText classifiers trained on Wikipedia/OpenWebText. While effective for general web-crawls, these filters often penalize domain-specific data (e.g., legal briefs, clinical notes, or proprietary code) because specialized terminology and structural syntax are statistically treated as "low-quality" or "gibberish" relative to standard English. This results in the accidental removal of the most valuable training tokens for domain-specific models, forcing researchers to either accept high-noise datasets or manually curate small, expensive "gold" corpora.

#### 3. Core Hypothesis
A sample's utility for domain-specific pre-training is proportional to its "Semantic Density"—defined as the ratio of its alignment with a specialized domain manifold versus its alignment with a general-purpose linguistic manifold. By filtering data based on the *divergence* between a domain-specific encoder and a generalist encoder, we can isolate high-value specialized content that standard filters would otherwise discard.

#### 4. Method
The proposed SDCF workflow consists of four implementation milestones:
1.  **Seed Manifold Construction:** Identify a small "gold-standard" corpus (e.g., 500MB of peer-reviewed medical journals). Train a lightweight domain-specific BERT-style encoder ($E_{dom}$) on this seed.
2.  **Generalist Baseline:** Utilize a frozen, general-purpose encoder ($E_{gen}$) such as RoBERTa-base.
3.  **Contrastive Scoring:** For each candidate document $D$ in a noisy raw pool:
    *   Calculate the reconstruction error or the mean-pooled embedding distance to the domain centroid using $E_{dom}$.
    *   Calculate the same for $E_{gen}$.
    *   Assign a score $S = \text{dist}(D, E_{gen}) / \text{dist}(D, E_{dom})$.
4.  **Thresholding & Sampling:** Select documents with the highest $S$ scores. This prioritizes documents that are "well-structured" in the domain context but "outliers" in the general context.

#### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Target Domain:** Biomedicine.
*   **Source Pool:** The "Pile-CC" (Common Crawl) subset of the Pile, which contains significant noise.
*   **Gold Seed:** PubMed Central Open Access subset.
*   **Downstream Evaluation:** The PubMedQA and MedQA (USMLE) benchmarks.

#### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Filtering Efficiency:** The ratio of "tokens kept" to "downstream accuracy gain" (Accuracy per Billion Tokens).
*   **Perplexity:** Zero-shot perplexity on a held-out set of high-quality medical textbooks.
*   **Downstream Task Performance:** Accuracy on MedQA and MMLU-Medical subtasks after fine-tuning a base model (e.g., Llama-3-8B) on the filtered data.

#### 7. Baselines
*   **Heuristic-based:** KenLM perplexity filtering (standard CCNet approach).
*   **Classifier-based:** A fastText classifier trained to distinguish "Medical" vs "Non-medical" using Wikipedia categories.
*   **Random Sampling:** A control group using an unfiltered subset of the same size.

#### 8. Ablations
*   **Seed Size Sensitivity:** Testing the method with 10MB, 100MB, and 1GB of "gold" seed data to determine the minimum required for an effective manifold.
*   **Encoder Architecture:** Comparing the use of simple TF-IDF vectors versus Transformer-based embeddings for the $E_{dom}$ and $E_{gen}$ components.
*   **Static vs. Dynamic Thresholding:** Comparing a fixed top-K cutoff versus a percentile-based distribution cutoff.

#### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Domain Narrowing:** The filter may become *too* specific, selecting only documents that mirror the "gold seed" exactly, leading to a loss of linguistic diversity and poor generalization (overfitting the filter).
*   **Computational Overhead:** Running two encoders over multi-terabyte datasets is computationally expensive compared to fastText.
    *   *Mitigation:* Use dimensionality reduction (PCA) on embeddings or use a "two-stage" approach where fastText narrows the pool before SDCF is applied.
*   **Seed Bias:** If the gold seed contains specific formatting artifacts (e.g., LaTeX strings), the filter may learn to prefer "formatting" over "knowledge."
    *   *Mitigation:* Aggressive de-biasing of the seed data via regex-based normalization before manifold construction.

Research Proposal: Adaptive Difficulty Filtering for Domain-Specific Language
Model Pretraining## Title
AdaFilter: Adaptive Difficulty-Aware Data Filtering for
Domain-Specific Language Model Pretraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Domain-specific language models (e.g., BioBERT, CodeBERT, FinBERT,
Legal-BERT) are typically pretrained from scratch or continually trained on a
curated corpus of in-domain text. A critical but understudied bottleneck is how
to filter which documents from the domain corpus are actually useful for
downstream performance. Current practice relies on heuristics (perplexity
thresholds, hand-crafted rules, or simple length/n-gram filters) that are noisy,
domain-agnostic, and oblivious to the model's current state during training. The
result is wasted compute on low-quality or redundant documents and, in some
cases, performance degradation from noisy data.

Concrete gap: No existing method jointly models (a) document quality, (b)
difficulty relative to the model's evolving capabilities, and (c) domain
relevance in a unified, trainable filtering pipeline. Prior work treats these
dimensions separately or uses static filtering that does not adapt during
training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A trainable, difficulty-aware filtering module that scores documents
along three axes — domain relevance, linguistic quality, and current-model
difficulty — and dynamically selects a curriculum of documents during
pretraining will produce a domain-specific LM with better perplexity and
downstream task performance than static heuristic filtering, while reducing
total training tokens by ≥20%.

Null hypothesis: Adaptive difficulty filtering yields no statistically
significant improvement in downstream performance over static heuristic
filtering (perplexity, F1, or accuracy) when matched for total compute.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
We propose AdaFilter, a three-stage filtering framework integrated into
the training loop.

Stage1: Relevance Scoring (one-time preprocessing)

Use a small, efficient classifier (e.g., a FastText or MiniLM-based model) to
score each document against a set of domain-defining seed keywords or exemplars.
This is a lightweight binary classifier trained on a small hand-labeled set (~1K
documents per domain). Documents below a relevance threshold are discarded
before training begins.

Stage2: Quality Scoring (one-time preprocessing)

For surviving documents, compute three quality signals:

• Perplexity under a small reference LM (e.g., a125M-parameter general-domain
model) — anomalously high PPL flags gibberish.
• Repetition ratio — fraction of repeated n-grams (n=8).
• Information density — ratio of unique tokens to total tokens. Combine into a
scalar quality score via a learned linear weighting (trained on a held-out
quality-labeled set).

Stage3: Adaptive Difficulty Curricula (online, per-epoch)

During training, maintain a difficulty estimator — a small MLP that takes the
model's current token-level embeddings for the first K tokens of a document and
predicts a difficulty score. Documents are bucketed into Easy/Medium/Hard bins.
The training sampler draws:

• **Epoch1-2:**80% Easy,15% Medium,5% Hard (warm-up)
• **Epoch3-5:**40% Easy,40% Medium,20% Hard- **Epoch6+:**10% Easy,40%
Medium,50% HardThe difficulty estimator is updated every N steps to track the
model's evolving state.

Training Protocol- Continual pretraining (MLM objective) starting from a
general-domain checkpoint (e.g., RoBERTa-base).

• Compare against: (a) unfiltered data, (b) static perplexity-filtered data,
(c) random subset of equal size, (d) random subset of equal compute.
• Each condition is run with3 random seeds for statistical reliability.
• Downstream evaluation every5K steps using a held-out set of domain tasks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
We propose two domains for generalizability:

1 Biomedical: CORD-19 + PubMed abstracts (~2M documents). Downstream: BioASQ
(QA), ChemProt (RE), PubMedQA.
2 Legal: Pile-of-Law subset + EURLex (~1M documents). Downstream: CaseHOLD
(NLI), LexGLUE benchmark.

Each domain provides a clean test of whether domain-specific filtering matters
beyond generic heuristics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Category | Metric | Target |

|---|---|---| | Language modeling | Validation perplexity | Primary | |
Downstream tasks | Macro F1 / Accuracy (domain-specific benchmarks) | Primary |
| Efficiency | Training tokens to match baseline best performance | Secondary |
| Curriculum effect | Per-bin difficulty distribution over epochs | Analysis | |
Ablation | Delta from removing each AdaFilter component | Diagnostic |

All metrics reported with95% confidence intervals across3 seeds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|---|---| | No Filter | All domain documents, no curation | | PPL Threshold |
Documents with PPL < median under general-domain LM | | Heuristic | Length +
n-gram repetition filter (common practice) | | Random Subset (size-matched) |
Same number of documents as AdaFilter, randomly sampled | | Random Subset
(compute-matched) | Same number of training steps as AdaFilter, randomly sampled
| | DSIR | Importance resampling using n-gram hashing (Xie et al.,2023) | |

Research Proposal: Structured Memory Banks for Long-Context Grounding in LLMs##
Title
Memory-Augmented Hierarchical Summarization (MAHS): Improving Long-Context
Grounding Without Full Attention Retraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Large Language Models suffer from the lost-in-the-middle problem — when
prompted with documents exceeding ~8K tokens, accuracy on facts located in the
middle of the context degrades sharply, even for models that claim128K+ context
windows. Two root causes: (1) softmax attention dilutes signal across many
tokens, and (2) positional encodings (RoPE, ALiBi) lose relative resolution at
extreme lengths. Existing solutions (ring attention, sparse attention,
state-space models) either require expensive full retraining or sacrifice recall
on mid-context facts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Injecting a separately trained, retrieval-augmented memory bank —
built from hierarchically compressed chunks of the input context — into the
LLM's cross-attention layers will recover mid-context fact recall to within90%
of short-context performance without fine-tuning the base LLM. The memory bank
acts as a "second path" that bypasses diluted full-context attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
Component1 — Hierarchical Chunking & Summarization

• Split the input context into fixed-size chunks (e.g.,512 tokens each).
• For each chunk, generate a short natural-language summary (<=64 tokens) using
a lightweight LM (e.g., Phi-3-mini). This forms the first summary layer.
• Recursively apply the same process to the summary sequence to produce a
second, coarser summary layer.
• Store all chunks and summaries in a flat key-value store keyed by chunk
position and semantic embedding.

Component2 — Retrieval-Augmented Memory Attention

• Insert a small set of memory tokens (e.g.,128) at the start of each attention
layer's key-value cache during generation.
• At each decoding step, retrieve the top-k chunks/summaries (by cosine
similarity to the current hidden state) from the memory bank.
• Encode the retrieved chunks as additional key-value pairs appended to the
existing full-context KV cache for that layer, but with a separate learned
gating scalar that down-weights the full-context path when memory retrieval
has high confidence.

Component3 — Training (Lightweight)

• Freeze the base LLM entirely.
• Train only the memory encoder (a small transformer, ~50M params), the
retrieval projection layer, and the gating scalars.
• Training objective: next-token prediction on long-document perplexity, with
an auxiliary contrastive loss that pulls the hidden state closer to the
embedding of the chunk containing the ground-truth next token.

Base model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (128K context)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Purpose | Metric |

|-----------|---------|--------| | RULER (Hsieh et al.,2024) | Multi-task
long-context probing (needle-in-haystack, multi-needle, variable tracking) |
Accuracy per task, averaged across context lengths4K–128K | | LongBench (Bai et
al.,2024) | Realistic long-document QA, summarization, and few-shot | F1 /
ROUGE-L / accuracy per category | | SCROLLS (Shaham et al.,2022) | Long
narrative & legal document QA | F1 | | Custom: Mid-Context Perturbation Set | A
constructed50K-token corpus where every question's answer appears only in the
middle third (positions33%–66%) | F1 gap relative to same question with answer
in first10% |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary: Accuracy on RULER's multi-needle task at64K
and128K context lengths.

2 Secondary:

• Perplexity on held-out long documents (16K–128K).
• Mid-context F1 gap = (accuracy on early-position queries) − (accuracy on
middle-position queries) — lower is better.
• Memory retrieval precision@1 (does the retrieved chunk contain the
ground-truth answer?).

3 Efficiency: Wall-clock time per generation token vs. baseline Llama-3.1 full
attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|----------|-----| | Base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (full attention,128K) |
Reference point for lost-in-the-middle | | Llama-3.1 with chunked
cross-attention (no memory, no retrieval) | Ablates the retrieval component | |
LongLoRA fine-tune on long documents | Ablates the "no fine-tuning" claim | |
InfLLM (sparse attention + retrieval) | Closest published method; shows whether
memory bank approach improves over retrieval-only | | GraphRAG / MemWalker
(summarize-then-retrieve) | Tests whether hierarchical summarization alone
(without retrieval gating) is sufficient |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. No hierarchical summaries — flat chunk retrieval only. Tests whether
the summary hierarchy matters.

equally. Tests whether the learned down-weighting is essential.
3 Memory bank size sweep —32,64,128,256 memory tokens. Characterizes the
trade-off between compute overhead and recall.
4 k retrieval sweep — top-1, top-3, top-5 chunks retrieved. Tests sensitivity
to retrieval depth.
5 Base model size — repeat best configuration on Llama-3.1-70B to test scaling
behavior.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation in Proposal |

|---|---| | Retrieval noise — retrieved chunks are irrelevant, wasting memory
tokens and confusing the decoder | Contrastive loss in training; gating scalar
can down-weight low-confidence retrievals | | Summary information loss —
compressed summaries lose critical entity/relation details | Two-layer hierarchy
with flat chunks as fallback; both are stored and retrievable | | Memory token
overhead kills speed —128 extra tokens ×32 layers creates latency blowup | Only
insert memory tokens at the last ~8 layers (ablate this design choice);
benchmark wall-clock time explicitly | | No improvement over InfLLM —
retrieval-only methods already capture mid-context facts | If so, the result is
still publishable: lightweight memory bank training is insufficient without
architecture changes; report negative result | | Positional embedding mismatch —
retrieved chunks lack correct positional IDs, confusing the base model | Use a
learned positional offset based on the chunk's original position in the
document; if this fails, try position-invariant retrieval (RoPE-free encoding) |
| Contrastive loss collapses — all chunk embeddings converge to a single point |
